questions.explanation: Original sum = 25 × 8 = 200. New sum = 24 × 9 = 216. The 9th number = 216 − 200 = 16.
questions.trap: Students may confuse 'mean decreased' with the new number being 25 − 24 = 1, or may add the difference (25−24=1) to 25 to get 26. The correct method computes both totals then subtracts.

questions.question:
A set contains the five values 2, 4, 6, 8, and n, where n > 6.
Column A: Mean of the set
Column B: Median of the set
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — pin down the median. Since n > 6, when the set is sorted n lands in the 4th or the 5th position, so the middle (3rd) value is always 6. Column B = 6, whatever n is.
Step 2 — the mean is (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + n)/5 = (20 + n)/5.
Step 3 — the mean beats 6 exactly when 20 + n > 30, that is when n > 10.
Step 4 — test both sides of that threshold, staying inside n > 6:
n = 7 gives mean = 27/5 = 5.4, which is LESS than the median 6, so Column B is greater.
n = 20 gives mean = 40/5 = 8, which is MORE than 6, so Column A is greater.
Two legal values of n give opposite answers, so the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Choosing A on the reasoning that n could be enormous and would drag the mean up. All we are told is n > 6, and every n from just above 6 up to 10 leaves the mean BELOW the fixed median of 6. On any mean-versus-median comparison with a free variable, test one value just inside the constraint and one far outside it before committing.

questions.question: Class A has 10 students with a mean score of 78. Class B has 15 students with a mean score of 88. What is the mean score of all 25 students combined? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — turn each average into a total. Class A: 10 x 78 = 780. Class B: 15 x 88 = 1320.
Step 2 — combine: total score = 780 + 1320 = 2100 over 25 students.
Step 3 — 2100/25 = 84.
Faster route (alligation): Class B holds 15 of the 25 students, or 3/5 of them, so the combined mean sits 3/5 of the way along the 10-point gap from 78 to 88: 78 + 0.6 x 10 = 84.
Check: 25 x 84 = 2100. Correct.
Answer: 84.
questions.trap: Averaging the two averages: (78 + 88)/2 = 83. That is legal only when the two groups are the same size. Class B is larger, so the combined mean must lie closer to 88 than to 78 - and 84 is indeed 6 above 78 but only 4 below 88.

questions.question: The set {5, 9, 12, 16, 18} has a mean of 12 and a median of 12. If the value 18 is replaced by 30, what happens to the mean and median?
options: B. Mean increases; median stays the same
C. Median increases; mean stays the same
E. Mean stays the same; median increases
questions.explanation: Original: sorted {5,9,12,16,18}, mean=60/5=12, median=12. Replace 18 with 30: new set {5,9,12,16,30}. New mean = (5+9+12+16+30)/5 = 72/5 = 14.4. New median: sorted {5,9,12,16,30}, 3rd value = 12. Median unchanged. So mean increases, median stays the same.
questions.trap: Students may assume that changing the largest value always affects both mean and median. The median only changes if the replacement alters which value sits in the middle position.

questions.question: The mean of a set of 5 positive integers is 10. Select all values that COULD be the median of this set.
questions.explanation: Total sum = 10 × 5 = 50. The median is the 3rd value when sorted. For each candidate: A (median=4): {1,1,4,22,22}, sum=50 ✓. B (median=8): {1,1,8,20,20}, sum=50 ✓. C (median=10): {1,1,10,19,19}, sum=50 ✓. D (median=14): {1,1,14,17,17}, sum=50 ✓. E (median=20): The 3rd, 4th, and 5th values must each be ≥ 20, so minimum sum ≥ 1+1+20+20+20 = 62 > 50. Impossible. Answer: A, B, C, D.
questions.trap: Students may assume the median can be anything as long as the mean constraint is met. But for the median to be 20, the three largest values must all be ≥ 20, which forces a sum exceeding 50.

questions.question:
A value equal to the mean is added to the set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.
Column A: Mean of the new 6-element set
Column B: Mean of the original 5-element set
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Original mean = (2+4+6+8+10)/5 = 30/5 = 6. The value added equals the mean = 6. New sum = 30+6 = 36. New count = 6. New mean = 36/6 = 6. Adding a value equal to the mean never changes the mean.
questions.trap: Students may think adding any new value changes the mean. Adding a value exactly equal to the current mean leaves the mean unchanged — this is a key GRE conceptual fact.

questions.question: The median of {3, 7, x, 15, 19} is 10, where the set is not yet sorted. Which of the following is a possible value of x?
questions.explanation: For a sorted 5-element set, median = 3rd value = 10. Since we need x to be the 3rd value when sorted, x must be ≥ 7 and ≤ 15 (so it lands in the middle position). If x = 10: sorted = {3,7,10,15,19}, median = 10 ✓. Check other options: x=2: sorted {2,3,7,15,19}, median=7 ✗. x=5: sorted {3,5,7,15,19}, median=7 ✗. x=12: sorted {3,7,12,15,19}, median=12 ✗. x=20: sorted {3,7,15,19,20}, median=15 ✗.
questions.trap: Students may try x=12 since 12 'looks like it should be near the middle', not realizing the median depends on where x falls in the sorted order, not just its approximate size.

questions.question: Group X has 20 people with a mean age of 35. Group Y has 30 people with a mean age of 45. What is the weighted mean age of the combined group?
questions.explanation: Total age for Group X = 20 × 35 = 700. Total age for Group Y = 30 × 45 = 1350. Combined total = 700 + 1350 = 2050. Total people = 50. Weighted mean = 2050 / 50 = 41.
questions.trap: Simple average of the two means gives (35+45)/2 = 40, which is wrong because Group Y is larger. The correct answer 41 is closer to 45 (the mean of the larger group).

questions.question: The mean of seven numbers is 14. When an eighth number is added, the mean becomes 15. What is the eighth number?
questions.explanation: Sum of 7 numbers = 14 × 7 = 98. New sum of 8 numbers = 15 × 8 = 120. Eighth number = 120 − 98 = 22.
questions.trap: Students may try 15 + (15−14) × 7 = 22 through indirect reasoning (correct but risky). The direct trap is computing 15 − 14 = 1 and reporting 1 as the eighth number.

options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Set P is already sorted: {1,3,5,7,9,11}. Count = 6 (even), so median = average of 3rd and 4th values = (5+7)/2 = 6. Mean = (1+3+5+7+9+11)/6 = 36/6 = 6. Both equal 6.
questions.trap: Students who use only the 3rd value (5) for the median of an even-count set get 5, leading them to choose Column B. Always average the two middle values for even-count sets.

questions.question: The set {p, p, 8, 14, q} has a mean of 10, where p and q are positive integers. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: B. p is a mode of the set
D. The median of the set is 8
questions.explanation:
The count is 5 and the mean is 10, so the sum is 5 x 10 = 50: p + p + 8 + 14 + q = 50.
A - that simplifies to 2p + q = 28. TRUE.
B - p occupies two of the five slots. The only way another value could match that is if q equals 8 or 14, and then it too appears exactly twice - never more. So no value ever appears more often than p, which makes p a mode (sometimes one of two). TRUE.
C - take p = 10, forcing q = 28 - 20 = 8. Then q < p. FALSE.
D - with p = 10 and q = 8 the sorted set is {8, 8, 10, 10, 14} and the median is 10, not 8. FALSE.
E - q is a positive integer, so q >= 1 and 2p = 28 - q <= 27, giving p <= 13.5, so p <= 13. TRUE.
Answer: A, B, E.
questions.trap: Rejecting B by reading it as 'p is the ONLY mode' - with p = 7 the set is {7, 7, 8, 14, 14}, which is bimodal, yet p is still a mode. C and D both look safe because the set is written in what appears to be increasing order; it is not sorted, and p can be larger than q and larger than 8. E is the one most people skip: the fact that q must be at least 1 is what caps p.

questions.question: The average (arithmetic mean) of five consecutive even integers is 18. What is the largest of the five integers?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — consecutive even integers are evenly spaced, and for an evenly spaced set mean = median. So 18 is the MIDDLE (3rd) term.
Step 2 — build the list outward from 18 in steps of 2: 14, 16, 18, 20, 22.
Step 3 — the largest is two steps above the middle: 18 + 2 x 2 = 22.
Check: (14 + 16 + 18 + 20 + 22)/5 = 90/5 = 18. Correct.
Answer: 22.
questions.trap: Choice E adds five steps to the mean, 18 + 2 x 5 = 28, and choice D adds four, 18 + 8 = 26, as if 18 were the first term. The mean of an evenly spaced set sits in the middle, so the largest term is only two steps - 4 - above it. Choice A is the mean itself.

questions.question: The median of a sorted list of 7 values is 42. The first three values are 10, 25, and 38. The last three values are 55, 67, and 80. What is the value of the 4th element (the median)?
questions.explanation: For a sorted list of 7 values, the median is the 4th value. We are told the median is 42. Therefore the 4th value = 42.
questions.trap: This is a reading comprehension check. The median of a 7-element sorted list IS the 4th element, and the problem states the median is 42. Students who attempt complicated calculations miss this direct fact.

questions.question: A dataset of 10 numbers has a mean of 50. If each number in the dataset is increased by 5, what is the new mean?
questions.explanation: If every value increases by 5, the total sum increases by 5 × 10 = 50. New mean = (500 + 50) / 10 = 550/10 = 55. Equivalently, the mean shifts by the same amount added to each value: 50 + 5 = 55.
questions.trap: Students may multiply the original mean by 5 to get 250, confusing 'increase each value by 5' with 'multiply each value by 5'. Adding a constant to all values shifts the mean by that constant.

questions.question:
The ages of five employees are 24, 28, 31, 35, and 42.
Column A: Mean age of the five employees
Column B: Median age of the five employees
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.trap: Students may eyeball a symmetric distribution and assume mean = median. The value 42 is further from 31 than 24 is, creating a slight right skew that pulls the mean above the median.

questions.question: A set of 6 numbers has a mean of 12 and a median of 11. Which of the following statements must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The sum of all 6 numbers is 72
B. At least one number is greater than 12
D. The 3rd and 4th values (when sorted) average to 11
questions.explanation: A: Sum = mean × count = 12 × 6 = 72. TRUE. B: Mean (12) > median (11), suggesting right skew; if all values were ≤ 12 then the mean could not exceed the median when the median is 11 — at least one value must exceed 12 to pull the mean above the median. TRUE. C: Mode might be 11 but is not guaranteed — the set could be {5,8,10,12,14,23} where no mode exists. FALSE. D: For a sorted 6-element set, median = average of 3rd and 4th values = 11. This is the definition. TRUE. E: A number could be negative; nothing prevents this. FALSE.
questions.trap: Statement C is the classic trap: students assume the median value must also be the mode. These are independent properties.

questions.question: In the set {2, 5, 8, 11, x}, x is a positive integer and the mean of the set equals the median of the set. What is x?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the four known values sum to 2 + 5 + 8 + 11 = 26, so the mean is (26 + x)/5.
Step 2 — the median depends on where x lands. Try the case x >= 11: then the sorted set is {2, 5, 8, 11, x} and the median is the 3rd value, 8.
Step 3 — set mean = median: (26 + x)/5 = 8, so 26 + x = 40 and x = 14.
Step 4 — check the case holds together: 14 >= 11, so the sorted set really is {2, 5, 8, 11, 14}. Mean = 40/5 = 8 and median = 8. Correct.
(If x were allowed to be a non-integer, the case 5 <= x <= 8 would make x itself the median and give (26 + x)/5 = x, so 4x = 26 and x = 6.5. That is why the stem restricts x to integers.)
Answer: 14.
questions.trap: Choice E, 40, is the total the five numbers must reach, not the missing value - subtract the 26 already present. Choice A comes from dividing by 4 instead of 5, and choice B is the average of the four known values. Choice C sets x equal to the median without checking the mean: with x = 8 the set is {2, 5, 8, 8, 11}, whose mean is 34/5 = 6.8, not 8.

questions.question: A shop's sales, in units, on seven consecutive days were 12, 20, 12, 25, 20, 12, and 15. What is the sum of the median and the mode of these seven values? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — sort before touching the median: 12, 12, 12, 15, 20, 20, 25.
Step 2 — with 7 values the median is the 4th one: 15.
Step 3 — count frequencies: 12 appears three times, 20 appears twice, 15 and 25 appear once each. The mode is 12.
Step 4 — median + mode = 15 + 12 = 27.
Answer: 27.
questions.trap: Reading the median off the unsorted list, whose 4th entry is 25, and answering 25 + 12 = 37. The second slip is calling 20 the mode because it is the largest repeated value - frequency alone decides the mode, and 12 appears three times to 20's two, which would give 15 + 20 = 35.

questions.question: The mean of four numbers is 25. A fifth number is added to the set, and the mean of the five numbers is 23. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — old total = 25 x 4 = 100.
Step 2 — new total = 23 x 5 = 115.
Step 3 — the fifth number is the difference between the two totals: 115 - 100 = 15.
Check: (100 + 15)/5 = 115/5 = 23. Correct.
Faster route: the new number has to drag all five values down by 2 each, a total pull of 5 x 2 = 10, so it must sit 10 below the old mean: 25 - 10 = 15.
Answer: 15.
questions.trap: Choice A reports the drop in the mean (2) as the number itself, and choice D is the new mean minus that drop. The subtle error is choice C: spreading the 2-point drop over only the four OLD numbers, 25 - 2 x 4 = 17. The new mean applies to all five values, so the deficit to cover is 2 x 5 = 10.

questions.question:
n is a positive integer.
Set A = {n, n+2, n+4, n+6, n+8}
Column A: Mean of Set A
Column B: Median of Set A
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Set A is 5 consecutive even-spaced values with common difference 2. It is symmetric around the middle term n+4. Mean = (n + n+2 + n+4 + n+6 + n+8)/5 = (5n+20)/5 = n+4. Median = 3rd value of sorted set = n+4. Both equal n+4 for any positive integer n.
questions.trap: Students may not recognize that an arithmetic sequence is symmetric, so mean = median = middle term. They may try specific values and get the right answer accidentally, or they may assume the relationship depends on n.

questions.question: If each value in a dataset is multiplied by 3, which of the following is TRUE?
options: A. The mean is multiplied by 3; the median is unchanged
B. The median is multiplied by 3; the mean is unchanged
C. Both the mean and median are multiplied by 3
D. Neither the mean nor the median changes
E. The mean increases by 3; the median increases by 3
questions.explanation: Multiplying every value by 3 scales the entire dataset by a factor of 3. Mean: new sum = 3 × old sum; new mean = 3 × old mean. Median: the sorted order is unchanged; the middle value(s) are each tripled; new median = 3 × old median. Both measures of center scale by 3.
questions.trap: Students may confuse scaling (multiply by constant) with shifting (add constant). Adding a constant shifts mean and median by that constant. Multiplying by a constant scales both mean and median by that constant.

questions.question: The mean of {6, 9, 12, 15, 18, x} is 12. What is x?
questions.trap: Students who compute the mean of the 5 known values (60/5 = 12) and then say 'x could be anything' make an error. There is exactly one value of x that satisfies the equation.

questions.question: Set S = {4, 8, 8, 10, 20}. Set T is formed by adding 6 to each value of S. Set U is formed by multiplying each value of S by 6. Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The mean of T is 6 greater than the mean of S
B. The median of T equals the median of S
C. The range of T equals the range of S
D. The mode of U is 48
E. The range of U is 6 greater than the range of S
questions.explanation:
First describe S: it is already sorted, so mean = 50/5 = 10, median = 8 (3rd of 5), mode = 8, range = 20 - 4 = 16.
T = {10, 14, 14, 16, 26} and U = {24, 48, 48, 60, 120}.
A - mean of T = 80/5 = 16 = 10 + 6. Adding a constant shifts the mean by that constant. TRUE.
B - median of T = 14, while the median of S is 8. A shift moves the median too. FALSE.
C - range of T = 26 - 10 = 16, the same as the range of S. Every value moved by the same amount, so the gap between the largest and the smallest is untouched. TRUE.
D - in U the value 48 appears twice and everything else once, so the mode is 48 = 6 x 8. Scaling multiplies the mode. TRUE.
E - range of U = 120 - 24 = 96, which is 6 TIMES the range of S, not 6 more than it. FALSE.
Answer: A, C, D.
questions.trap: B and E swap the two rules. Adding a constant moves the centre (mean, median, mode) but leaves the spread (range, standard deviation) alone; multiplying by a constant scales the centre AND the spread. Picking B treats the median as if it were a measure of spread; picking E treats multiplication as if it were addition.

questions.question: The average (arithmetic mean) of five numbers is 30. The average of the three largest is 36 and the average of the three smallest is 25. What is the median of the five numbers?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — write the sorted values as a <= b <= c <= d <= e. The median is c.
Step 2 — turn every average into a sum:
all five: a + b + c + d + e = 5 x 30 = 150
three smallest: a + b + c = 3 x 25 = 75
three largest: c + d + e = 3 x 36 = 108
Step 3 — add the two group sums: 75 + 108 = 183. That total counts each of a, b, d, e exactly once, but counts c TWICE, because the middle value belongs to both groups.
Step 4 — so 183 = (a + b + c + d + e) + c = 150 + c, giving c = 33.
Check: a + b = 75 - 33 = 42 and d + e = 108 - 33 = 75, so the set could be 20, 22, 33, 37, 38 - sum 150, three smallest averaging 25, three largest averaging 36. Correct.
Answer: 33.
questions.trap: Choice B, 30, assumes the median must equal the mean. It is the overlap that pins the answer down: the two groups share the middle value, so 75 + 108 - 150 = 33. Choice C averages the two group means, (25 + 36)/2 = 30.5, and choices A and E simply report one of the group averages.

questions.question:
A set of 10 positive integers has a mean of 15 and a median of 12.
Column A: The sum of the 5 largest values
Column B: The sum of the 5 smallest values
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the whole set: sum = 10 x 15 = 150. The two columns split that total, so Column A + Column B = 150.
Step 2 — use the median. For 10 sorted values the median is the average of the 5th and 6th, so the 5th value + the 6th value = 24. Since the 5th is no larger than the 6th, the 5th value is at most 12.
Step 3 — every one of the 5 smallest values is at most the 5th value, hence at most 12. So Column B <= 5 x 12 = 60.
Step 4 — therefore Column A = 150 - Column B >= 150 - 60 = 90.
Column A is at least 90 while Column B is at most 60, so Column A is greater no matter what the actual numbers are.
questions.trap: Choosing D because no individual values are given. Two facts settle it: the median caps each of the bottom five at 12 (at most 60 altogether), while the mean fixes the whole set at 150. Whenever a set's mean sits above its median, the weight of the set is in its upper half.

questions.question: Team A has 8 players with a mean height of 72 inches. Team B has 12 players with a mean height of 75 inches. The two teams merge into a single 20-player team, and then one player whose height is 70 inches leaves. What is the mean height, in inches, of the remaining players? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — convert each average into a total. Team A: 8 x 72 = 576 inches. Team B: 12 x 75 = 900 inches.
Step 2 — merged team: sum = 576 + 900 = 1476 over 20 players (a mean of 73.8).
Step 3 — the departure changes BOTH the sum and the count: new sum = 1476 - 70 = 1406, new count = 20 - 1 = 19.
Step 4 — 1406/19 = 74.
Check: 19 x 74 = 1406. Correct.
Answer: 74.
questions.trap: Subtracting the 70 from the total but still dividing by 20, which gives 1406/20 = 70.3. When a member leaves, the count must fall with the sum. A second error is averaging the two team means, (72 + 75)/2 = 73.5, which ignores that Team B has more players and so pulls the merged mean toward 75.

questions.question: A set of 9 values has a mean of 40 and a median of 35. The largest value in the set is then increased by 30, and nothing else changes. Which of the following describes the new mean and the new median?
options: A. The mean increases by 30; the median is unchanged
B. The mean increases by 30/9; the median is unchanged
C. The mean increases by 30/9; the median increases by 30/9
D. The mean increases by 30/9; the median increases by 30
E. Both the mean and the median increase by 30
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the mean. Old sum = 9 x 40 = 360. Raising one value by 30 makes the new sum 390.
Step 2 — new mean = 390/9 = 43.33..., which is 40 + 30/9 = 40 + 3.33. The extra 30 is shared out over all 9 values, so the mean rises by 30/9, not by 30.
Step 3 — the median. With 9 sorted values the median is the 5th. The value that changed was already the largest and it only got larger, so no value changes rank and the 5th value is still 35.
The mean rises by 30/9; the median does not move.
Answer: B.
questions.trap: Choice A adds the whole 30 to the mean, forgetting that a mean divides by the count. Choices C, D and E move the median: the median depends only on POSITION, and pushing the top value further up changes no ranks at all. Had the largest value been DECREASED by 30 it could have fallen past the middle, and then the median would have moved.

questions.question: A set of 5 distinct positive integers has a mean of 18 and a median of 16. The smallest value is 8 and the largest is 30. What is the greatest possible value of the second largest number in the set? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — sum = 5 x 18 = 90. Sorted, the set looks like {8, b, 16, d, 30}, where 8 < b < 16 < d < 30.
Step 2 — the sum equation: 8 + b + 16 + d + 30 = 90, so b + d = 90 - 54 = 36.
Step 3 — d is largest when b is smallest. The integers are distinct and b must sit strictly between 8 and 16, so the smallest b can be is 9.
Step 4 — d = 36 - 9 = 27.
Check: {8, 9, 16, 27, 30} - five distinct positive integers, sum 90, mean 18, median 16, and 27 is still below the largest value 30. Correct.
Answer: 27.
questions.trap: Answering 36, which is the SUM b + d rather than either value on its own. The other slip is allowing b = 8 (which would give d = 28): the integers are distinct, so the second value must be at least 9. And d = 27 is only legal because it stays under the stated largest value, 30.

questions.question:
A set of 6 positive integers has a mean of 10, and its two smallest values are each equal to 1.
Column A: The greatest possible value of the median of the set
Column B: 11
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — sum = 6 x 10 = 60. Two of the values are 1, so the other four sum to 58. Call them v3 <= v4 <= v5 <= v6.
Step 2 — with 6 sorted values the median is (v3 + v4)/2, so the job is to make v3 + v4 as large as possible.
Step 3 — the ceiling comes from the top pair: v5 and v6 are each at least v4, so v5 + v6 >= 2 x v4 >= v3 + v4. Since (v3 + v4) + (v5 + v6) = 58, that forces v3 + v4 <= 29.
Step 4 — 29 is not reachable with integers: it would need v4 >= 15, leaving only 29 for v5 + v6 while both must be at least 15. So try 28: v3 = v4 = 14 and v5 = v6 = 15 gives {1, 1, 14, 14, 15, 15}, which sums to 1 + 1 + 14 + 14 + 15 + 15 = 60. Valid.
Step 5 — the greatest possible median is 28/2 = 14, and 14 > 11. Column A is greater.
questions.trap: Assuming the median cannot exceed the mean of 10 and choosing B. Two values are pinned at 1, which frees a large share of the total for the middle of the set. The real ceiling comes from the requirement that the two values ABOVE the median be at least as large as the median's own pair - that is what caps v3 + v4 at 28.

questions.question: The mean of a list of 10 numbers is 20. One additional number is added to the list, and the mean of the resulting 11 numbers is an integer. Which of the following could be the number that was added? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the original list sums to 10 x 20 = 200.
Step 2 — after adding x the list has 11 numbers, so the new mean is (200 + x)/11. That is an integer exactly when 200 + x is a multiple of 11.
A - 200 + 9 = 209 = 11 x 19, so the new mean is 19. TRUE.
B - 200 + 20 = 220 = 11 x 20, so the new mean is 20; adding a value equal to the mean leaves the mean alone. TRUE.
C - 200 + 30 = 230, and 230/11 = 20.909..., not an integer. FALSE.
D - 200 + 31 = 231 = 11 x 21, so the new mean is 21. TRUE.
E - 200 + 50 = 250, and 250/11 = 22.727..., not an integer. FALSE.
Answer: A, B, D.
questions.trap: Choices C and E are exactly the values that make the new SUM a multiple of 10 - the OLD count. Once the eleventh number joins, the divisor is 11. Notice the workable additions sit 11 apart: 9, 20, 31, 42, 53, and so on.

questions.question: The mean of 12 numbers is 15. The mean of the first 5 of them is 12, and the mean of the last 4 is 18. What is the mean of the remaining 3 numbers?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — total sum = 12 x 15 = 180.
Step 2 — first group: 5 x 12 = 60. Last group: 4 x 18 = 72.
Step 3 — the remaining 3 numbers must supply 180 - 60 - 72 = 48.
Step 4 — their mean = 48/3 = 16.
Check: 60 + 72 + 48 = 180 across 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 values. Correct.
Answer: 16.
questions.trap: Choice E is the leftover sum, 48, reported before dividing by 3; choice A divides that 48 by 4 instead of 3. The conceptual trap is choice B: assuming a leftover group must average the overall mean. It would only do so if the two known groups already averaged 15 between them - in fact they average (60 + 72)/9 = 14.67, so the final three have to come in above 15 to compensate.

questions.question:
A set S contains n values (n > 1) with mean M and median Q. A new value exactly equal to M is added to S.
Column A: New mean of S after adding the value
Column B: New median of S after adding the value
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: New mean: adding M to a set with mean M leaves the mean unchanged = M. New median: the median shifts when a new value is inserted. The new median depends on whether M is above, below, or equal to Q (the original median). Case 1: M = Q. Adding M shifts the median slightly but it remains M = Q, so new median = M = new mean. Case 2: M > Q (right-skewed). Adding M (which is above Q) may shift the median up toward M but not necessarily to M. The new median could be below M, making Column A (M) > Column B. Case 3: M < Q (left-skewed). Adding M (below Q) shifts median down, potentially below M, giving Column B > Column A. So the relationship depends on the original distribution. Answer: D.
questions.trap: Students may assume that since the mean stays constant at M and M is added, the median must also stay constant. But inserting M changes which values occupy the middle position(s).

questions.question: A set of 8 numbers has a mean of 30. When its largest and its smallest values are both removed, the remaining 6 numbers have a mean of 28. The largest value is 5 times the smallest. What is the largest value? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — total sum = 8 x 30 = 240.
Step 2 — the 6 survivors sum to 6 x 28 = 168.
Step 3 — so the two removed values together account for 240 - 168 = 72.
Step 4 — with L = 5S, the pair is 5S + S = 6S = 72, so S = 12 and L = 5 x 12 = 60.
Check: 168 + 12 + 60 = 240, and 240/8 = 30. Also 60 = 5 x 12, and 60 and 12 are indeed the largest and smallest. Correct.
Answer: 60.
questions.trap: Answering 72, which is the combined value of the two removed numbers rather than the larger one. The other slip is splitting 72 by dividing by 5 (giving 14.4): the two pieces are 5 parts and 1 part, so there are 6 parts in total and each part is 12.

questions.question: Section 1 has 20 students with a mean score of 72. Section 2 has n students with a mean score of 84. When the two sections are combined, the mean score of all the students is 80. What is n?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — write the combined mean as one equation in sums:
(20 x 72 + 84n)/(20 + n) = 80
Step 2 — clear the denominator: 1440 + 84n = 1600 + 80n.
Step 3 — 4n = 160, so n = 40.
Faster route (alligation): the combined mean of 80 sits 8 above Section 1's mean and 4 below Section 2's. The group sizes go in the INVERSE ratio of those gaps, so Section 1 : Section 2 = 4 : 8 = 1 : 2. With 20 students in Section 1, Section 2 has 40.
Check: (1440 + 40 x 84)/60 = (1440 + 3360)/60 = 4800/60 = 80. Correct.
Answer: 40.
questions.trap: Choice B, 20, assumes the sections must be the same size. They cannot be: equal sizes would put the combined mean at (72 + 84)/2 = 78, not 80. The combined mean sits twice as far from 72 as it does from 84, so the group averaging 84 must be twice as large.

options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Sorted Set T = {4, 7, 7, 9, 13}. Median = 3rd value = 7. Mean = (4+7+7+9+13)/5 = 40/5 = 8. Column A (8) > Column B (7).
questions.trap: Students may notice 7 appears twice (as the mode) and assume the median equals the mode equals some 'central' value, then compare to a vaguely-estimated mean. Always compute both exactly.

questions.question: A set of 8 integers has a mean of 25. Which of the following changes to the set would leave the mean exactly 25? Select all that apply.
options: A. Adding one new value equal to 25
B. Multiplying every value in the set by 2
C. Adding two new values whose sum is 50
D. Increasing one value by 12 and decreasing another value by 12
E. Adding 25 to one of the values
questions.explanation:
The set starts with sum = 8 x 25 = 200 across 8 values.
A - new sum 225 across 9 values: 225/9 = 25. Adding a value equal to the mean never moves the mean. TRUE.
B - new sum 400 across 8 values: 400/8 = 50. Scaling every value scales the mean by the same factor. FALSE.
C - new sum 250 across 10 values: 250/10 = 25. The two new values average 25 between them, so they behave like two copies of the mean. TRUE.
D - the sum stays at 200 (the +12 and the -12 cancel) and the count stays at 8: 200/8 = 25. TRUE.
E - new sum 225 across 8 values: 225/8 = 28.125. FALSE.
Answer: A, C, D.
questions.trap: A and E look like the same move and are not: adding 25 AS a new member raises the sum and the count in step, while adding 25 TO an existing member raises the sum with no extra member to absorb it. B is the other bait - doubling every value doubles the mean rather than preserving it.

questions.question: In a data set of n numbers the mean is 50. One value of 80 is replaced by a value of 20, and the mean falls by 3. What is n?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — find the change in the sum. Swapping 80 for 20 removes 80 - 20 = 60 from the total, and the count does not change.
Step 2 — a drop of 60 in the sum lowers the mean by 60/n.
Step 3 — set that equal to the stated drop: 60/n = 3, so n = 20.
Check: with n = 20 the old sum is 20 x 50 = 1000; the new sum is 940, and 940/20 = 47 = 50 - 3. Correct.
Answer: 20.
questions.trap: Choice E is the drop in the SUM and choice D is the new mean - neither answers 'how many numbers'. Choice A uses the wrong gap: 80 - 50 = 30 measures the removed value's distance from the mean, but what actually leaves the total is 80 - 20 = 60, the distance between the old and new values. Choice C halves that 60 because two values were 'involved', though only one slot changed.

questions.question: A teacher records 10 test scores. The mean is 74 and the median is 70. The teacher then discovers that one score was recorded as 56 instead of the correct 86. After correction, what is the new mean?
questions.explanation: Original sum = 74 × 10 = 740. Changing the mis-recorded 56 to the correct 86 adds 30, giving 770. New mean = 770/10 = 77. (The median is irrelevant.)
questions.trap: Students may use the median (70) in their calculation, or divide by 9 instead of 10 thinking the corrected score is a new addition. The median is a red herring; only the sum and count matter.

questions.question: A set of 2n numbers, listed from least to greatest as a1 <= a2 <= ... <= a2n, has mean M and median K, where M > K. Each of the n smallest values is replaced by the number M. Which of the following describes the mean and the median of the new set?
options: A. The mean increases and the median increases
B. The mean is unchanged and the median increases
C. The mean increases and the median is unchanged
D. The mean decreases and the median increases
E. Both the mean and the median are unchanged
questions.explanation:
Two facts to set up: the whole set sums to 2nM, and K = (a_n + a_{n+1})/2, so a_n <= K <= a_{n+1}.
Step 1 — the bottom half is small. Each of a1 ... a_n is at most a_n, and a_n <= K, so the bottom half sums to at most nK, which is strictly less than nM (because K < M).
Step 2 — the mean. Replacing that bottom half with n copies of M swaps a total of at most nK for a total of exactly nM, so the sum strictly rises while the count stays at 2n. The mean INCREASES above M.
Step 3 — the median. In the new set, n values equal M and every survivor is at least a_{n+1} >= K. So at most n of the 2n values can be K or below, which means the (n+1)th smallest value is strictly above K while the nth smallest is at least K. Their average - the new median - is therefore strictly greater than K. The median INCREASES.
Concrete check: {1, 1, 10, 12} has M = 24/4 = 6 and K = (1 + 10)/2 = 5.5, so M > K. Replacing the two smallest with 6 gives {6, 6, 10, 12}: mean = 34/4 = 8.5 > 6 and median = (6 + 10)/2 = 8 > 5.5. Both rose.
Answer: A.
questions.trap: Choice B is the magnet: replacing values with the mean 'should' leave the mean alone. It only would if the replaced values already averaged M, and here they are the bottom half of a set whose mean sits above its median, so they averaged strictly less - swapping them for M lifts the total. Choice C fails for the sister reason: the median is built from the top of the bottom half, so rewriting the bottom half does move it.

questions.question: A set of 5 positive integers has a mean of 16, a median of 15, and a unique mode of 12 that appears exactly twice. What is the greatest possible value of the largest number in the set? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — sum = 5 x 16 = 80. Write the sorted set as v1 <= v2 <= v3 <= v4 <= v5, with v3 = 15 since the median of 5 values is the 3rd.
Step 2 — locate the two 12s. Everything from position 3 onward is at least 15, so neither 12 can sit at position 3, 4 or 5. Both must sit at the bottom: v1 = v2 = 12.
Step 3 — the sum: 12 + 12 + 15 + v4 + v5 = 80, so v4 + v5 = 41.
Step 4 — to maximise v5, minimise v4. We know v4 >= 15, but v4 = 15 would make 15 a second value appearing twice, so the set would be bimodal and 12 would no longer be the UNIQUE mode. Hence v4 >= 16.
Step 5 — v4 = 16 gives v5 = 41 - 16 = 25.
Check: {12, 12, 15, 16, 25} has sum 80 (mean 16), median 15, and 12 is the only value appearing more than once. Correct.
Answer: 25.
questions.trap: Answering 26 by taking v4 = 15. That set, {12, 12, 15, 15, 26}, has two values appearing twice, so 12 is not the unique mode. The other error is letting a 12 sit at position 3 or 4: with a median of 15, every value from the third slot on is at least 15, which pins both 12s to the bottom two slots.

questions.question:
A company has 100 employees. The mean salary is $60,000, the median salary is $50,000, and the highest-paid employee earns $500,000. That employee's salary is then changed to $60,000, and no other salary changes.
Column A: The new mean salary
Column B: The new median salary
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — Column A is pinned exactly. Old total = 100 x 60,000 = 6,000,000. Replacing 500,000 with 60,000 removes 440,000, so the new total is 5,560,000 and the new mean is 5,560,000/100 = 55,600.
Step 2 — cap Column B. Sort the old salaries v1 <= v2 <= ... <= v100. The median says v50 + v51 = 100,000, and since v50 <= v51 the 50th salary is at most 50,000.
Step 3 — the new list is v1 ... v99 with 60,000 in place of v100. Because 60,000 is larger than v50 (which is at most 50,000), the bottom 50 positions are still v1 ... v50, and the 51st position is whichever is smaller, v51 or 60,000.
Step 4 — so the new median = (v50 + the smaller of v51 and 60,000)/2, which is at most (v50 + v51)/2 = 50,000.
Column A is exactly 55,600 and Column B is at most 50,000, so Column A is greater.
questions.trap: Choosing D because the individual salaries are unknown. The mean is fixed exactly and the median is capped by the old median - no arrangement of the other 99 salaries can push it past 50,000, so the comparison resolves without knowing a single value. Choosing C assumes the mean collapses onto the median once the outlier is gone; it does not, because the other 99 salaries have not moved.

questions.question: A set of 5 integers, not necessarily distinct, has a mean of 10, a smallest value of 4, and a range of 14. Which of the following could be the median of the set? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — range = largest - smallest, so the largest value is 4 + 14 = 18. Sum = 5 x 10 = 50.
Step 2 — sorted, the set is {4, a, m, b, 18} with 4 <= a <= m <= b <= 18, and 4 + a + m + b + 18 = 50, so a + m + b = 28.
Step 3 — how small can the median m be? Since a <= m and b <= 18, we get 28 = a + m + b <= m + m + 18, so 2m >= 10 and m >= 5.
Step 4 — how large can m be? Since a >= 4 and b >= m, we get 28 = a + m + b >= 4 + m + m, so 2m <= 24 and m <= 12.
Step 5 — so the median can be any integer from 5 to 12, and both ends are reachable.
A - 4 is below the floor. Concretely, a median of 4 forces the three smallest to be 4, 4, 4, so the fourth value would be 50 - 4 - 4 - 4 - 18 = 20, which exceeds the largest value 18. FALSE.
B - 5 works: {4, 5, 5, 18, 18} has sum 50, median 5, smallest 4, largest 18. TRUE.
C - 9 works: {4, 6, 9, 13, 18} has sum 50 and median 9. TRUE.
D - 12 works: {4, 4, 12, 12, 18} has sum 50 and median 12. TRUE.
E - 14 is above the ceiling of 12. With m = 14 the remaining two values satisfy a + b = 28 - 14 = 14, but a >= 4 and b >= m = 14, so a + b >= 18. Impossible. FALSE.
Answer: B, C, D.
questions.trap: Both wrong choices come from forgetting that the median is squeezed from both sides. Choice A ignores that the two values ABOVE the median plus the 18 must still fit inside a total of 50; choice E ignores that the two values BELOW the median cannot drop under 4. Fixing the range at 14 also fixes the maximum at exactly 18 - it is an equation, not a lower bound.

questions.question: A set of n integers has mean μ. Every integer in the set is increased by k. Then every integer in the new set is multiplied by m. In terms of μ, k, and m, what is the final mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Add k to every value. New mean = μ + k (adding a constant shifts the mean by that constant). Step 2: Multiply every value by m. New mean = m(μ + k) (multiplying every value by a constant scales the mean by that constant). Final mean = m(μ + k). Option A (mμ + k) is the result of multiplying first then adding — wrong order of operations. Option C (μ + mk) is the result of adding k×m without the initial shift — incorrect. Option D divides instead of multiplies. Option E uses m².
questions.trap: Students may apply the operations in reverse order (multiply first, then add) getting mμ + k (option A). The correct order is add k first, then multiply by m.

questions.question:
Three groups have the following data:
- Group 1: 10 values, mean = 20
- Group 2: 20 values, mean = 30
- Group 3: 30 values, mean = 40
A fourth group of 40 values is added. After adding Group 4, the overall mean of all 100 values is 36. What is the mean of Group 4?
questions.explanation: Sum of Groups 1+2+3: 10×20 + 20×30 + 30×40 = 200 + 600 + 1200 = 2000. Total students in Groups 1–3 = 60. Total for all 100 values: 36 × 100 = 3600. Sum of Group 4 = 3600 − 2000 = 1600. Mean of Group 4 = 1600/40 = 40. Verify: overall mean = (2000+1600)/100 = 3600/100 = 36 ✓.
questions.trap: Students who compute the simple average of the four group means (20+30+40+?)/4 = 36 → ? = 54 get the wrong answer. Weighted mean requires weighting by group size.

questions.question:
The numbers a1 <= a2 <= ... <= a2n, where n >= 2, are such that the average of the n smallest equals the average of the n largest, and each of those two averages is M.
Column A: The mean of all 2n numbers
Column B: The median of all 2n numbers
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — Column A. The bottom half sums to nM and the top half sums to nM, so all 2n numbers sum to 2nM and the mean is 2nM/(2n) = M.
Step 2 — Column B looks unpinned, but the sorted order hides a very strong consequence. Pair each bottom value with the top value the same distance along the list: a1 with a_{n+1}, a2 with a_{n+2}, and so on up to a_n with a_2n. Because the list is sorted, a_i <= a_{n+i} for every i from 1 to n.
Step 3 — add those n inequalities: a1 + ... + a_n <= a_{n+1} + ... + a_2n. We are told both sides equal nM, so the sum of the inequalities is actually an equality - which can only happen if EVERY one of them is an equality. Hence a_i = a_{n+i} for all i.
Step 4 — combine that with the sorted order: a1 = a_{n+1} forces a1 = a2 = ... = a_{n+1}, and the same chain carries through to a_2n. Every value in the set is the same number, and since the mean is M, every value equals M.
Step 5 — the median of a list whose values are all M is M.
Column A = Column B = M. The two quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Choosing D on the grounds that no actual numbers are given. The condition is far stronger than it looks: for a SORTED list, the bottom half can match the top half's total only if the two halves agree value by value, which collapses the whole set to one repeated number. Drop the sorting and the conclusion dies - the six numbers 0, 1, 29 (mean 10) and 9, 9, 12 (mean 10) also have overall mean 10, but their median is 9.

questions.question: In a class of 40 students, 25 play soccer and 20 play basketball. If 10 students play both sports, how many students play at least one of the two sports?
questions.explanation: Use inclusion-exclusion: |Soccer ∪ Basketball| = |Soccer| + |Basketball| - |Soccer ∩ Basketball| = 25 + 20 - 10 = 35. So 35 students play at least one sport.
questions.trap: Students add 25 + 20 = 45 without subtracting the overlap of 10, double-counting students who play both sports.

questions.question: A survey of 50 people found that 30 like coffee and 25 like tea. If 12 people like both, how many people like neither coffee nor tea?
questions.explanation: First find those who like at least one: |Coffee ∪ Tea| = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43. Then neither = Total - at least one = 50 - 43 = 7.
questions.trap: Students forget the 'neither' group and answer 12 (the overlap) or compute 50 - 30 - 25 + 12 = 7 correctly but then second-guess themselves.

questions.question: In a group of 60 students, 35 study French and 28 study Spanish. Every student studies at least one of the two languages. How many students study both French and Spanish? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — read the 'every student studies at least one' clause. It says neither = 0, so the union is the whole group: French or Spanish = 60.
Step 2 — inclusion-exclusion: (French or Spanish) = French + Spanish - both.
60 = 35 + 28 - both
Step 3 — solve: both = 63 - 60 = 3.
Check the four regions: French only 32, Spanish only 25, both 3, neither 0. Total 32 + 25 + 3 = 60. Correct.
Answer: 3.
questions.trap: Answering 63, the raw sum 35 + 28, and treating it as a headcount. Sixty-three people cannot exist in a group of 60 - the 3-person excess IS the overlap, because those 3 were counted once in each language.

questions.question: In a class, 18 students play chess and 14 students play checkers. Exactly 6 students play both games. How many students play chess but not checkers?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the 18 is a TOTAL, not an 'only'. It already contains the 6 who also play checkers.
Step 2 — chess only = chess total - both = 18 - 6 = 12.
Check: chess only 12 + both 6 = 18, the full chess count. Correct.
Answer: 12.
questions.trap: Choosing 18 by reading 'play chess' as 'play only chess'. Choice B, 8, is the same mistake made on the other set: 14 - 6 = 8 is checkers only, the wrong circle. Choice A, 6, reports the overlap itself.

questions.question: A gym has 100 members. 60 members use the pool, 50 members use the gym floor, and 20 members use both. How many members use neither facility?
questions.explanation: At least one facility: 60 + 50 - 20 = 90. Neither = 100 - 90 = 10.
questions.trap: Students compute 100 - 60 - 50 + 20 = 10 but others mistakenly compute 100 - 60 - 50 = -10 (ignoring overlap) and choose an incorrect option.

questions.question:
In a school of 80 students, 45 are in the math club and 40 are in the science club. Every student is in at least one club.

Column A: Number of students in both clubs
Column B: 5
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Since every student is in at least one club, neither = 0. So Total = |Math| + |Science| - |Both|. 80 = 45 + 40 - |Both|. |Both| = 85 - 80 = 5. Column A = 5 and Column B = 5, so the two quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Students may rush and say Column A is greater without computing the exact value. Careful calculation shows |Both| = 5, which equals Column B.

questions.question: Of 30 people surveyed, 20 own a car, 15 own a bicycle, and 5 own neither. How many people own both a car and a bicycle?
questions.explanation: Those who own at least one = 30 - 5 = 25. By inclusion-exclusion: 25 = 20 + 15 - |Both|. |Both| = 35 - 25 = 10.
questions.trap: Students forget to subtract 'neither' first. They use Total = 30 instead of 25 (those with at least one), leading to |Both| = 20 + 15 - 30 = 5 (wrong).

questions.question: In a survey of 200 people, 120 read newspaper A and 90 read newspaper B. If 40 people read both newspapers, how many people read at least one newspaper?
questions.trap: Students add 120 + 90 = 210 without subtracting 40, getting 210 instead of 170. The 40 who read both are counted in both the 120 and the 90.

questions.question: A club has 50 members. 30 speak English, 25 speak French, and 10 speak both. How many members speak only French?
questions.explanation: Only French = |French| - |Both| = 25 - 10 = 15.
questions.trap: Students confuse |French| (which is 25) with 'only French' (which is 15). The 10 bilingual speakers are included in the 25 French speakers.

questions.question:
In a class of 50 students, 28 like math, 22 like science, and 10 like both subjects.
Column A: The number of students who like math but not science
Column B: The number of students who like science but not math
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — math only = 28 - 10 = 18.
Step 2 — science only = 22 - 10 = 12.
Step 3 — 18 > 12, so Column A is greater.
Check the whole class: 18 + 12 + 10 = 40 in at least one subject, so 10 like neither. All regions are non-negative, so the data is consistent.
Answer: A.
questions.trap: Choosing C on the idea that removing the same 10 from each set leaves them tied. Subtracting the SAME number from two different totals preserves the gap: 28 - 22 = 6 before, 18 - 12 = 6 after. The difference never disappears.

questions.question: Of 100 students surveyed, 55 have a dog, 40 have a cat, and 15 have both a dog and a cat. How many students have neither a dog nor a cat?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — union first: dog or cat = 55 + 40 - 15 = 80.
Step 2 — neither is everything outside that union: 100 - 80 = 20.
Check the four regions: dog only 40, cat only 25, both 15, neither 20. They sum to 100. Correct.
Answer: 20.
questions.trap: Computing 100 - 55 - 40 = 5, choice A. That subtracts the 15 double-counted pet owners twice, so it removes too much. Either subtract the union (80) once, or write 100 - 55 - 40 + 15 = 20 to add the overlap back. Choice B, 10, is the sign error on that last term: 100 - 55 - 40 - 15 = -10, reported as 10. Choice C, 15, copies the overlap itself, and choice E, 25, is the cat-only region, 40 - 15, which answers a different question.

questions.question: In a group of 40 people, 24 own a smartphone and 18 own a tablet. Which of the following could be the number of people who own both a smartphone and a tablet? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Let x be the number who own both. Two bounds squeeze x.
Upper bound: the overlap cannot be larger than the smaller set, so x <= min(24, 18) = 18.
Lower bound: the union is 24 + 18 - x = 42 - x, and the union cannot exceed the 40 people who exist, so 42 - x <= 40, giving x >= 2.
So 2 <= x <= 18.
A - 0 is below 2. FALSE.
B - 2 is exactly the minimum, reached when nobody owns neither. TRUE.
C - 10 is inside the range. TRUE.
D - 18 is exactly the maximum, reached when every tablet owner also owns a smartphone. TRUE.
E - 20 exceeds the 18 tablet owners. FALSE.
Answer: B, C, D.
questions.trap: Selecting A because 'they might not overlap at all'. Since 24 + 18 = 42 is greater than 40, there is not enough room to keep the two groups apart: at least 42 - 40 = 2 people must be in both. Selecting E is the mirror error - forgetting that the overlap lives inside the smaller set.

questions.question: In a school, 40% of 200 students play a sport, 30% play a musical instrument, and 10% do both. How many students do neither?
questions.explanation: Convert percentages to counts: Sport = 40% × 200 = 80; Instrument = 30% × 200 = 60; Both = 10% × 200 = 20. At least one = 80 + 60 - 20 = 120. Neither = 200 - 120 = 80.
questions.trap: Students add 40% + 30% - 10% = 60%, then compute neither as 40% of 200 = 80 — actually correct! But some students compute 100% - 60% = 40%, then 40% × 200 = 80. Others forget to convert and work with raw percentages throughout.

questions.question: In a survey of 150 people, 85 like action movies, 70 like comedy movies, and 30 like neither genre. How many people like both action and comedy?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — strip out the 'neither' group before touching the formula. People who like at least one genre = 150 - 30 = 120.
Step 2 — inclusion-exclusion on that union: 120 = 85 + 70 - both.
Step 3 — both = 155 - 120 = 35.
Check the four regions: action only 50, comedy only 35, both 35, neither 30. Total 150. Correct.
Answer: 35.
questions.trap: Using the grand total 150 as the union: 85 + 70 - 150 = 5, choice A. The 30 who like neither are inside the 150 but outside the union, so the union is 120. Choice B, 30, is copying the 'neither' count; choice D, 50, is the action-only region, 85 - 35, which answers a different question; choice E, 120, stops at the union itself.

questions.question: Of 120 employees at a company, 75 have health insurance, 60 have dental insurance, and 20 have neither. How many employees have only health insurance (not dental)?
questions.explanation: At least one = 120 - 20 = 100. |Both| = 75 + 60 - 100 = 35. Only health insurance = 75 - 35 = 40.
questions.trap: Students answer 75 - 20 = 55 (subtracting 'neither' from |Health| instead of the overlap of 35). The correct two-step approach: first find |Both| using the union formula, then subtract from |Health|.

questions.question:
A group of 90 people: 50 drink coffee, 45 drink tea, and 15 drink neither.

Column A: Number who drink only coffee
Column B: Number who drink only tea
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: At least one drink = 90 - 15 = 75. |Both| = 50 + 45 - 75 = 20. Only coffee = 50 - 20 = 30. Only tea = 45 - 20 = 25. Column A (30) > Column B (25).
questions.trap: Students compare 50 vs 45 directly and assume the same ordering holds for 'only' values, but neglect to actually subtract the same overlap from each. The computation confirms Column A is greater: 30 vs 25.

questions.question: In a class of 80 students, 60% study Biology, 50% study Chemistry, and 20% study neither. What percentage of students study both Biology and Chemistry?
questions.explanation: At least one subject = 100% - 20% = 80%. By inclusion-exclusion: 80% = 60% + 50% - both%. Both% = 110% - 80% = 30%.
questions.trap: Students compute 60% + 50% = 110%, observe it exceeds 100%, and subtract 100% to get 10%. They forget to first account for the 20% who study neither (the union is 80%, not 100%).

questions.question: A survey asked 200 people about two social media platforms. 130 use Facebook, 95 use Instagram, and 25 use neither platform. How many people use exactly one of the two platforms?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — union: at least one platform = 200 - 25 = 175.
Step 2 — overlap: 175 = 130 + 95 - both, so both = 225 - 175 = 50.
Step 3 — 'exactly one' is the union minus the people counted in both circles: 175 - 50 = 125.
Long route, same answer: Facebook only = 130 - 50 = 80, Instagram only = 95 - 50 = 45, and 80 + 45 = 125.
Check: 80 + 45 + 50 + 25 = 200. Correct.
Answer: 125.
questions.trap: Answering 175, choice E - that is 'at least one', which still contains the 50 dual users. Choice A, 75, comes from subtracting the overlap twice (175 - 100); choice B, 80, stops at Facebook only; choice D, 150, subtracts the 50 from the grand total 200 instead of from the union.

questions.question: In a group of 100 workers, 60 can operate machine A, 47 can operate machine B, and 18 can operate neither. How many workers can operate exactly one machine?
questions.explanation: At least one machine = 100 - 18 = 82. |Both| = 60 + 47 - 82 = 25. Only machine A = 60 - 25 = 35. Only machine B = 47 - 25 = 22. Exactly one = 35 + 22 = 57. (Equivalently: 82 - 25 = 57.)
questions.trap: Students add |A| + |B| = 107 and treat that as the 'exactly one' count, or they compute union - neither = 82 and report 82 as the answer, forgetting to subtract those who operate both machines.

questions.question:
In a class, 40% of students passed Math, 35% passed Science, and 15% passed both.

Column A: Percentage who passed at least one subject
Column B: 60%
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: |Math ∪ Science| = 40% + 35% - 15% = 60%. Column A = 60% = Column B.
questions.trap: Students add 40% + 35% = 75% and choose Column A is greater (75% > 60%). They forget to subtract the 15% overlap.

questions.question: In a survey of 100 people, 70 like Brand X and 60 like Brand Y. Select all values that COULD represent the number of people who like neither brand.
questions.explanation: Let n = neither. Then at least one = 100 - n. By inclusion-exclusion: both = 70 + 60 - (100 - n) = 30 + n. Constraints: both ≥ 0 → always true; both ≤ min(70, 60) = 60 → 30 + n ≤ 60 → n ≤ 30; and n ≥ 0. So 0 ≤ n ≤ 30. Check: A(0): valid. B(5): valid. C(20): valid. D(30): valid — gives both = 60, which equals min(70,60). E(35): 30 + 35 = 65 > 60 = min(70,60). Invalid. Answer: A, B, C, D.
questions.trap: Students only check the lower bound (both ≥ 0) and miss the upper bound from the smaller set: both cannot exceed min(70,60) = 60, which caps neither at 30. Option E (n=35) would require both = 65 > 60, which is impossible.

questions.question: A school offers Drama and Art clubs. Of 90 students, 48 are in Drama, 36 are in Art, and 12 are in both. How many students are in neither club?
questions.explanation: At least one club = 48 + 36 - 12 = 72. Neither = 90 - 72 = 18.
questions.trap: Students compute 90 - 48 - 36 = 6 (subtracting both groups from total without adding back the overlap of 12). Must use the formula: neither = 90 - (48 + 36 - 12) = 18.

questions.question: In a neighborhood of 250 households, 60 percent subscribe to a streaming service. Of the households that subscribe to a streaming service, one third also subscribe to a cable service. 40 households subscribe to neither service. How many households subscribe to a cable service?
questions.explanation:
Build the 2x2 table; the cable total is a column sum, so find both cells of that column.
Step 1 — streaming households = 0.60 x 250 = 150.
Step 2 — the one third is taken of the STREAMING group, not of the neighborhood: both = (1/3) x 150 = 50. So streaming but no cable = 150 - 50 = 100.
Step 3 — the non-streaming row has 250 - 150 = 100 households, of which 40 have neither service, so cable but no streaming = 100 - 40 = 60.
Step 4 — cable total = 50 + 60 = 110.
Check the table: 50 + 100 + 60 + 40 = 250. Correct.
Answer: 110.
questions.trap: Answering 60, choice B - that is cable-only, and it omits the 50 cable subscribers who also stream. Choice A, 50, reports the overlap; choice C, 100, reports streaming-only; choice E, 150, applies the one third to the wrong base by treating the whole streaming count as the cable count.

questions.question:
In a study, 70 percent of participants exercise regularly, 60 percent maintain a healthy diet, and 10 percent do neither.
Column A: The percent of participants who both exercise regularly and maintain a healthy diet
Column B: 40%
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — union: at least one healthy habit = 100% - 10% = 90%.
Step 2 — inclusion-exclusion: 90 = 70 + 60 - both.
Step 3 — both = 130 - 90 = 40%.
Column A = 40% = Column B, so the quantities are equal.
Check the four regions: exercise only 30, diet only 20, both 40, neither 10. They sum to 100. Correct.
Answer: C.
questions.trap: Computing 70 + 60 - 100 = 30 by treating the whole population as the union and choosing B. The union is only 90%, because the 10% who do neither sit outside both circles. Every extra percent in 'neither' pushes the overlap UP by the same amount.

questions.question: A bookstore surveyed 180 customers about two categories of books. 110 customers bought fiction, and 45 of those 110 also bought non-fiction. Of the customers who did not buy fiction, 40 percent bought non-fiction. How many of the 180 customers bought neither category?
questions.explanation:
Set up the 2x2 table with fiction as the rows and non-fiction as the columns.
Step 1 — the fiction row: 110 total, 45 of them also bought non-fiction, so fiction-only = 110 - 45 = 65.
Step 2 — the no-fiction row: 180 - 110 = 70 customers.
Step 3 — the 40 percent belongs to that row, not to the whole survey: non-fiction only = 0.40 x 70 = 28.
Step 4 — neither = 70 - 28 = 42.
Check the table: both 45 + fiction only 65 + non-fiction only 28 + neither 42 = 180. Correct.
Answer: 42.
questions.trap: Applying the 40 percent to all 180 customers: 0.40 x 180 = 72, choice E. The percent is stated for the customers who did NOT buy fiction, a 70-person row. Choice B, 28, stops at the non-fiction-only cell; choice A, 25, comes from 180 - 110 - 45, which subtracts the overlap out of the wrong row.

questions.question: In a class of 50 students, 30 study French and 25 study German. Every student studies at least one of the two languages. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. Exactly 5 students study both languages
B. At least 5 students study both languages
C. More students study only French than study only German
D. Exactly 20 students study only French
E. Exactly 45 students study only French
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — 'every student studies at least one' forces neither = 0, so the union is 50.
Step 2 — 50 = 30 + 25 - both, so both = 55 - 50 = 5. The overlap is pinned exactly, not merely bounded.
Step 3 — French only = 30 - 5 = 25; German only = 25 - 5 = 20; exactly one language = 25 + 20 = 45.
A - both is exactly 5. TRUE.
B - 5 >= 5, so 'at least 5' also holds. TRUE.
C - 25 > 20. TRUE.
D - French only is 25; 20 is GERMAN only. FALSE.
E - 45 is the number who study exactly one language, not French only. FALSE.
Answer: A, B, C.
questions.trap: Rejecting A because the stem never says 'exactly'. The clause 'every student studies at least one' removes the last free variable, so the overlap is determined, not a range. D and E are the two nearby region values - German only (20) and exactly-one (45) - which catch students who compute the right numbers and then attach them to the wrong label.

questions.question: A hotel surveyed its guests: 40 percent ordered room service, 35 percent used the spa, and 25 percent used neither service. What percent of guests used both room service and the spa? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — union: used at least one service = 100% - 25% = 75%.
Step 2 — inclusion-exclusion: 75 = 40 + 35 - both.
Step 3 — both = 75 - 75 = 0%.
So no guest used both services: the 40% and the 35% happen to fit into the 75% union with nothing left over.
Check the four regions: room service only 40, spa only 35, both 0, neither 25. They sum to 100. Correct.
Answer: 0.
questions.trap: Refusing to accept 0 and forcing a positive overlap, usually by computing 40 + 35 - 100 = -25 and reporting 25. Zero overlap is a legitimate outcome whenever the two sets exactly fill the union; the formula tells you so, and 0 is a valid entry.

questions.question:
Group of 60 people: 35 like jazz, 30 like classical, 5 like neither.

Column A: Number who like jazz but NOT classical
Column B: Number who like classical but NOT jazz
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: At least one = 60 - 5 = 55. Both = 35 + 30 - 55 = 10. Jazz only = 35 - 10 = 25. Classical only = 30 - 10 = 20. Column A (25) > Column B (20).
questions.trap: Students compare 35 vs 30 directly and conclude Column A is greater for the wrong reason — but the computation confirms it. The risk is not computing 'only' values and comparing raw totals.

questions.question: In a survey of 500 people, 55 percent watch TV daily and 40 percent use social media daily. If 20 percent do neither, what percent watch TV daily but do NOT use social media daily?
questions.explanation:
Work entirely in percents; the 500 never enters the arithmetic because the answer is a percent.
Step 1 — union: at least one daily habit = 100 - 20 = 80%.
Step 2 — overlap: 80 = 55 + 40 - both, so both = 95 - 80 = 15%.
Step 3 — TV but not social media = TV total - both = 55 - 15 = 40%.
Check the four regions: TV only 40, social only 25, both 15, neither 20. They sum to 100. Correct.
Answer: 40%.
questions.trap: Answering 55%, choice E, by reading 'watch TV' as 'watch TV only'. Choice C, 35%, subtracts the 20% who do neither from the 55% - the wrong quantity: 'neither' sits outside both circles and never comes out of the TV count. Choice A is the overlap and choice B is social-media only.

questions.question: Of 240 athletes, some run and some swim. 150 run, 120 swim, and 30 do neither. How many athletes both run and swim?
questions.trap: Students forget to subtract 'neither' from the total and use 240 as the union: 150 + 120 - 240 = 30. The correct union is 210 (those with at least one activity), giving both = 60.

questions.question: In a city, 45% of residents speak English, 30% speak Spanish, and 10% speak both. What percentage of residents speak exactly one of these two languages?
questions.explanation: Only English = 45% - 10% = 35%. Only Spanish = 30% - 10% = 20%. Exactly one language = 35% + 20% = 55%. (Cross-check: union = 45+30-10 = 65%; exactly one = union - both = 65% - 10% = 55%. ✓)
questions.trap: Students add 45% + 30% = 75% and treat that as 'at least one,' then compute exactly one as 75% - 10% = 65%. But the correct union is 45+30-10 = 65%, and exactly one = 65% - 10% = 55%.

questions.question:
In a group of 100 people: 60 own a laptop, 50 own a tablet, and 20 own neither.

Column A: Number who own both a laptop and a tablet
Column B: 30
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: At least one = 100 - 20 = 80. Both = 60 + 50 - 80 = 30. Column A = 30 = Column B.
questions.trap: Students compute 60 + 50 - 100 = 10 (using total instead of the union of 80), concluding Column B is greater. The union is 80, not 100, because 20 people own neither.

questions.question: In a group of 80 students, 50 study Math and 40 study Physics. Some study both and some study neither. Which of the following are possible values for the number studying both? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Let b = both. The union = 50 + 40 - b = 90 - b must be ≤ 80 (cannot exceed total group), so b ≥ 10. Also b ≤ min(50, 40) = 40. So 10 ≤ b ≤ 40. Check: A(5): fails b ≥ 10. B(10): valid — union = 80, neither = 0. C(20): valid — union = 70, neither = 10. D(35): valid — union = 55, neither = 25. E(40): valid — union = 50, neither = 30 (all physics students also study math). Answer: B, C, D, E.
questions.trap: Students only apply the upper bound b ≤ 40 and choose all options except E (thinking b cannot equal the smaller set). They miss that b can equal min(50,40)=40. They also miss the lower bound: since 90 - b ≤ 80, b ≥ 10, ruling out A.

questions.question: In a school of 300 students, every student studies at least one of three subjects: math, science, or history. 160 study math, 140 study science, and 130 study history. 60 study both math and science, 50 study both math and history, and 40 study both science and history; each of these three pairwise counts includes the 20 students who study all three subjects. How many students study exactly one subject?
questions.explanation:
The pairwise numbers are TOTAL intersections, so each one already contains the 20 triple students.
Step 1 — confirm the data is consistent by computing the union: 160 + 140 + 130 - 60 - 50 - 40 + 20 = 430 - 150 + 20 = 300. That matches the 300 students, so nobody is left out. Correct.
Step 2 — peel the pairwise counts down to exactly-two regions: math and science only = 60 - 20 = 40; math and history only = 50 - 20 = 30; science and history only = 40 - 20 = 20. Exactly two = 40 + 30 + 20 = 90.
Step 3 — exactly one = total - exactly two - exactly three = 300 - 90 - 20 = 190.
Direct formula, same answer: exactly one = (sum of the three sets) - 2(sum of the pairwise) + 3(triple) = 430 - 300 + 60 = 190.
Check by region: math only = 160 - 60 - 50 + 20 = 70; science only = 140 - 60 - 40 + 20 = 60; history only = 130 - 50 - 40 + 20 = 60. 70 + 60 + 60 = 190. Correct.
Answer: 190.
questions.trap: Choice E, 210, comes from 300 - 90: removing the exactly-two students but leaving the 20 all-three students inside the 'exactly one' count. Choice A, 130, is 430 - 300, the formula run without the +3(triple) term; choice C, 170, uses +2(triple) instead of +3. Choice B, 150, is 300 - (60 + 50 + 40): treating the three pairwise counts as disjoint blocks of two-subject students and subtracting them straight from the total, which strips out the 20 all-three students three times over.

questions.question: In a survey of 200 people about three streaming services X, Y, and Z, 110 use X, 95 use Y, and 80 use Z. 45 use both X and Y, 35 use both X and Z, and 30 use both Y and Z; each of these pairwise counts includes everyone who uses all three services. Every person surveyed uses at least one of the three services. How many people use all three services? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — 'every person uses at least one' means the union is the whole survey: |X or Y or Z| = 200.
Step 2 — three-set inclusion-exclusion, with the pairwise numbers taken as full intersections:
200 = 110 + 95 + 80 - 45 - 35 - 30 + T
Step 3 — collect: 110 + 95 + 80 = 285 and 45 + 35 + 30 = 110, so 200 = 285 - 110 + T = 175 + T.
Step 4 — T = 200 - 175 = 25.
Check every region: X only = 110 - 45 - 35 + 25 = 55; Y only = 95 - 45 - 30 + 25 = 45; Z only = 80 - 35 - 30 + 25 = 40; XY only = 20; XZ only = 10; YZ only = 5; all three = 25. Sum = 55 + 45 + 40 + 20 + 10 + 5 + 25 = 200. Correct.
Answer: 25.
questions.trap: Stopping at 285 - 110 = 175 and reporting 175, or concluding that 0 people use all three because the formula 'came out' at 175. The triple term is the one unknown in the equation, and the 25-person gap between 175 and the 200-person union IS that term. The pairs subtract; the triple adds back.

questions.question: Of 500 adults surveyed, 60 percent drink coffee, 45 percent drink tea, and 25 percent drink both. One adult is chosen at random from among those who drink at least one of the two beverages. What is the probability that the chosen adult drinks tea?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — convert to counts: coffee = 0.60 x 500 = 300; tea = 0.45 x 500 = 225; both = 0.25 x 500 = 125.
Step 2 — the sample space is restricted to 'at least one beverage', so find that union: 300 + 225 - 125 = 400.
Step 3 — the favourable group is ALL tea drinkers, 225 of them, including the 125 who also drink coffee.
Step 4 — probability = 225/400 = 9/16.
Check the regions: coffee only 175, tea only 100, both 125, neither 100. They sum to 500, and 175 + 100 + 125 = 400. Correct.
Answer: 9/16.
questions.trap: Choice C, 9/20, uses all 500 adults as the denominator; the stem restricts the draw to the 400 who drink something. Choice A, 1/4, is 100/400, the probability of drinking ONLY tea; choice B, 5/16, is 125/400, the probability of drinking both; choice E, 3/4, is 300/400, the coffee answer.

questions.question:
In a class, 70 percent of the students passed exam A and 80 percent passed exam B. Nothing else is known about how the two groups overlap.
Column A: The smallest possible percent of the class that passed both exams
Column B: The largest possible percent of the class that passed neither exam
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — minimise the overlap for Column A. The union can never exceed 100%, so 70 + 80 - both <= 100, giving both >= 50%. The smallest possible overlap is 50%, reached when nobody fails both exams.
Step 2 — maximise 'neither' for Column B. Neither = 100 - union, so making 'neither' as large as possible means making the union as small as possible. The union can never be smaller than the larger of the two sets, so union >= 80%. The smallest union is 80%, reached when every exam-A passer also passed exam B, and then neither = 100 - 80 = 20%.
Step 3 — compare: 50% > 20%, so Column A is greater.
Note that the two scenarios describe different classes; each column is optimised on its own, which is exactly what 'smallest possible' and 'largest possible' ask for.
Answer: A.
questions.trap: Reading Column A as the LARGEST possible overlap, which is min(70, 80) = 70%, or reading Column B as the smallest 'neither', which is 0%. A second slip is computing the maximum 'neither' as 100 - 70 = 30% by shrinking the union to the wrong set - the union must contain the bigger set, 80%, not the smaller one.

questions.question: In a group of 120 people, 75 have taken a cooking class, 60 have taken a pottery class, and 45 have taken a painting class. 30 have taken both cooking and pottery, 25 have taken both cooking and painting, and 20 have taken both pottery and painting; each of these three pairwise counts includes the 10 people who have taken all three classes. Some people have taken none of the three. How many people have taken exactly two of the three classes? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — add the pairwise intersections: 30 + 25 + 20 = 75.
Step 2 — see what that sum actually counts. Someone in exactly two classes appears in exactly one of the three pairwise groups, so they are counted once. Someone in all three appears in all three pairwise groups, so they are counted three times.
So 75 = (exactly two) + 3 x (all three).
Step 3 — exactly two = 75 - 3 x 10 = 75 - 30 = 45.
Check by region: cooking only = 75 - 30 - 25 + 10 = 30; pottery only = 60 - 30 - 20 + 10 = 20; painting only = 45 - 25 - 20 + 10 = 10. Exactly-two regions: 20, 15, 10, which sum to 45. Union = 60 + 45 + 10 = 115, so 5 people took none - consistent with 120. Correct.
Answer: 45.
questions.trap: Answering 65, from 75 - 10: subtracting the all-three group once instead of three times. Each of those 10 people sits inside cooking-and-pottery, cooking-and-painting AND pottery-and-painting, so they are triple-counted in the 75 and must be removed three times over.

questions.question: A company has 400 employees, each of whom works at exactly one of three locations: the city office, remotely, or the satellite office. 50 percent work at the city office and 35 percent work remotely. Of the city office workers, 30 percent lead a team; of the remote workers, 20 percent lead a team; of the satellite office workers, 20 percent lead a team. What percent of the company's team leaders work at the city office?
questions.explanation:
This is a double matrix: location down the side, leads-a-team across the top. Fill the leader column one row at a time, because each percent applies to its own row.
Step 1 — row sizes: city = 0.50 x 400 = 200; remote = 0.35 x 400 = 140; satellite = 400 - 200 - 140 = 60.
Step 2 — leaders in each row: city = 0.30 x 200 = 60; remote = 0.20 x 140 = 28; satellite = 0.20 x 60 = 12.
Step 3 — total leaders = 60 + 28 + 12 = 100.
Step 4 — the question asks for a share OF THE LEADERS, so the base is 100, not 400: 60/100 = 60%.
Check: 60 + 28 + 12 = 100 leaders and 140 + 112 + 48 = 300 non-leaders, and 100 + 300 = 400. Correct.
Answer: 60%.
questions.trap: Choice D, 50%, assumes leaders are spread through the company in the same proportion as employees - but the city office has the highest leadership rate, so it is over-represented among leaders. Choice C, 30%, quotes the city leadership RATE instead of the city share of leaders; choice B, 25%, answers a different question (100 leaders out of 400 employees); choice A, 20%, is the remote rate.

questions.question:
In a large group of people, 65 percent like product A. Of the people who like product A, 40 percent also like product B. 10 percent of the group like neither product.
Column A: The percent of the group who like product B but not product A
Column B: 20%
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Set the group to 100 people and build the 2x2 table.
Step 1 — like A = 65.
Step 2 — the 40 percent is taken of the A group, not of the whole group: both = 0.40 x 65 = 26. So A but not B = 65 - 26 = 39.
Step 3 — the not-A row has 100 - 65 = 35 people. Of those, 10 like neither product, so B but not A = 35 - 10 = 25.
Step 4 — 25 > 20, so Column A is greater.
Check the table: both 26 + A only 39 + B only 25 + neither 10 = 100. Correct. (For reference, B's total is 26 + 25 = 51, which the stem never had to give.)
Answer: A.
questions.trap: Subtracting the wrong cell from the not-A row. That row holds 35 people and it is the 10 who like NEITHER product that come out of it; a student who subtracts the 26 'both' instead gets 35 - 26 = 9, which is below 20 and gives choice B. Choosing D on the grounds that B's overall percentage is never stated is the other slip - B's total is never needed, because the not-A row settles B-only in one subtraction. Remember too that the 40 percent is taken of the A group, not of the whole group, so 'both' is 26 and not 40.

questions.question: In a group of 100 people, 70 speak language A and 60 speak language B. No other information is given. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. At least 30 people speak both languages
B. At most 60 people speak both languages
C. At least 10 people speak neither language
D. At most 30 people speak neither language
E. If no one in the group speaks neither language, then exactly 30 people speak both
questions.explanation:
Let x be the number who speak both. Union = 70 + 60 - x = 130 - x, and neither = 100 - (130 - x) = x - 30.
A - the union cannot exceed 100, so 130 - x <= 100 and x >= 30. TRUE.
B - the overlap cannot exceed the smaller set, so x <= 60. TRUE.
C - neither = x - 30, and x can be exactly 30, which makes neither = 0. So 'at least 10 speak neither' is not forced. FALSE.
D - neither = x - 30 and x <= 60, so neither <= 30. TRUE.
E - if neither = 0 then the union is 100, so 130 - x = 100 and x = 30 exactly. TRUE.
Answer: A, B, D, E.
questions.trap: Selecting C by reasoning that 70 + 60 = 130 overshoots 100 by 30, so 30 people must be 'left over' outside the sets. The excess is absorbed by the OVERLAP, not by the 'neither' region: when exactly 30 speak both, the union is exactly 100 and nobody is left out. Note also that neither = both - 30 here, so the two regions move together, one always 30 behind the other.

questions.question: In a school of 80 students, every student belongs to at least one of three clubs: A, B, or C. Club A has 50 members, club B has 45 members, and club C has 38 members. Exactly 15 students belong to A and B but not C, exactly 12 belong to A and C but not B, and exactly 10 belong to B and C but not A. How many students belong to all three clubs? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
The three given numbers are EXACTLY-TWO counts, not full pairwise intersections, so the standard inclusion-exclusion formula does not apply as written. Use the membership-counting identity instead.
Step 1 — name the regions: let T be the number in all three. Exactly two = 15 + 12 + 10 = 37. Since every student is in at least one club, exactly one = 80 - 37 - T = 43 - T.
Step 2 — count club memberships. Adding the three club sizes counts a one-club student once, a two-club student twice, and a three-club student three times:
50 + 45 + 38 = (exactly one) + 2(exactly two) + 3T
133 = (43 - T) + 2(37) + 3T
133 = 43 - T + 74 + 3T = 117 + 2T
Step 3 — 2T = 16, so T = 8.
Check each club: A only = 50 - 15 - 12 - 8 = 15; B only = 45 - 15 - 10 - 8 = 12; C only = 38 - 12 - 10 - 8 = 8. Exactly one = 15 + 12 + 8 = 35, and 35 + 37 + 8 = 80. Correct.
Answer: 8.
questions.trap: Answering 16 by writing 133 - 117 = 16 and forgetting that T carries a coefficient of 2 in that equation.
