questions.question: Data sets X and Y each consist of 5 positive integers, and their standard deviations are equal: SD(X) = SD(Y) = s. Data set Z consists of all 10 values from X and Y together. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The mean of Z equals the average of the mean of X and the mean of Y.
B. The standard deviation of Z equals s.
C. The range of Z equals the range of X plus the range of Y.
D. If the mean of X equals the mean of Y, then the standard deviation of Z is at least s.
E. The range of Z is at least as large as the range of X.
questions.explanation:
A - mean(Z) = (sum of X + sum of Y)/10 = (5 x mean(X) + 5 x mean(Y))/10 = (mean(X) + mean(Y))/2. The simple average works here precisely because the two sets are the SAME size. TRUE.
B - false whenever the two sets are centred at different places. Take X = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and Y = {11, 12, 13, 14, 15}, both with SD sqrt(2) = 1.41. Then Z = {1, ..., 5, 11, ..., 15} has mean 8 and SD 5.20, far above 1.41. The 10-unit gap between the group means is itself a source of spread. FALSE.
C - ranges do not add. With X = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (range 4) and Y = {11, 12, 13, 14, 15} (range 4), Z spans 15 - 1 = 14, not 4 + 4 = 8. FALSE.
D - suppose mean(X) = mean(Y) = m. Then mean(Z) = m too, and every deviation in Z is measured from the same m it was measured from inside its own set. Sum of squared deviations for Z = 5s^2 + 5s^2 = 10s^2, so variance(Z) = 10s^2/10 = s^2 and SD(Z) = s exactly. 'At least s' includes equality, so the statement holds. TRUE.
E - Z contains every value of X plus five more, so max(Z) >= max(X) and min(Z) <= min(X). Subtracting, range(Z) >= range(X). TRUE.
Answer: A, D, E.
questions.trap: Selecting B by assuming that merging two equally spread sets preserves that spread. It does only when the two means coincide (that is exactly statement D); when the means differ, the distance between the group centres adds variance on top of the within-group variance. C is the mirror-image error on range - combining sets can leave a gap between them, so the combined range can far exceed the sum of the two.

questions.question: A data set of 10 values has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. A second data set of 10 values has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. The two data sets are combined into a single data set of 20 values. What is the standard deviation of the combined data set?
options: E. Cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the combined mean. The two groups are the same size, so it is the simple average: (10 x 50 + 10 x 70)/20 = 1200/20 = 60.
Step 2 — the idea. Each value's deviation from 60 has two parts: how far it sits from its OWN group mean, and how far its group mean sits from 60. Squared deviations add up as
sum of squared deviations = (within-group part) + (between-group part).
Step 3 — the within-group part. Each group has 10 values and SD 10, so each contributes 10 x 10^2 = 1000. Together: 2000.
Step 4 — the between-group part. Group 1's mean is 50 - 60 = -10 from the combined mean and group 2's is 70 - 60 = +10. Each of the 10 values in a group carries that group's offset, so each group contributes 10 x 10^2 = 1000. Together: 2000.
Step 5 — total sum of squared deviations = 2000 + 2000 = 4000, over 20 values.
Variance = 4000/20 = 200, so SD = sqrt(200) = 10 x sqrt(2) = 14.14.
Check with a concrete pair: take five 40s and five 60s (mean 50, SD 10) and five 60s and five 80s (mean 70, SD 10). Combined, the 20 values have mean 60 and squared deviations 400 (five times), 0 (five times), 0 (five times), 400 (five times) - total 4000, variance 200, SD 14.14. Correct.
Answer: 10 x sqrt(2).
questions.trap: Choice A, 10, is the assumption that two groups with the same SD merge into a set with that SD - it ignores the 20-unit gap between the group centres, which is itself spread. Choice C, 10 x sqrt(5), comes from measuring each group's offset from the combined mean as the full 20 instead of 10, giving 100 + 400 = 500. Choice D, 20, reads the gap between the means as the answer. Choice E gives up too early: because both groups are the same size and both SDs are given, the combined variance is fully determined even though the individual values are not.

questions.question: In a class, 10 students scored an average of 80 on a test and the other 15 students scored an average of 70. What was the average score of all 25 students?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — turn each average into a total. Averages cannot be combined directly; totals can.
Group of 10: 10 x 80 = 800.
Group of 15: 15 x 70 = 1050.
Step 2 — add the totals and divide by the total head count.
(800 + 1050)/25 = 1850/25 = 74.
Check the pull direction: the 15-student group is larger, so the combined mean must sit below the midpoint 75 and closer to 70. 74 does. Correct.
Answer: 74.
questions.trap: Averaging the averages: (80 + 70)/2 = 75, choice C. That would only be right if the two groups were the same size. Choice D, 76, is the same arithmetic with the weights attached to the wrong groups (15 x 80 + 10 x 70, all over 25).

questions.question: A store sells 3 items at $10 each and 7 items at $20 each. What is the weighted average price per item?
questions.explanation: Total revenue: (3 × $10) + (7 × $20) = $30 + $140 = $170. Total items: 3 + 7 = 10. Weighted average price = $170 / 10 = $17.
questions.trap: Students average $10 and $20 to get $15, ignoring the different quantities. The 7 items at $20 carry more weight, pulling the average above $15.

questions.question: A course grade is computed from two components: a quiz worth 1 credit and an exam worth 2 credits. A student scores 90 on the quiz and 60 on the exam. What is the student's weighted average score? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the credits are the weights: 1 for the quiz, 2 for the exam, total 3.
Step 2 — weighted average = (1 x 90 + 2 x 60)/(1 + 2).
= (90 + 120)/3 = 210/3 = 70.
Check: the exam carries two thirds of the weight, so the answer must sit two thirds of the way from 90 down toward 60, that is 90 - (2/3)(30) = 70. Correct.
Answer: 70.
questions.trap: Answering 75, the plain average of 90 and 60. The exam counts twice, so the mean is dragged toward 60, not parked halfway. Answering 80 is the same slip with the weights swapped: (2 x 90 + 1 x 60)/3 = 80.

questions.question: The weighted average of 4 and 8 with weights 3 and 1, respectively, is:
questions.trap: Students compute (4 + 8) / 2 = 6, ignoring the weights entirely. The weight of 3 on the value 4 pulls the average much closer to 4.

questions.question:
A school has two classes. Class A has 20 students with an average score of 75. Class B has 20 students with an average score of 85.

Column A: The weighted average score of all 40 students
Column B: 80
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: When the two groups have EQUAL sizes, the weighted average is the same as the simple average. Weighted average = (20 × 75 + 20 × 85) / (20 + 20) = (1500 + 1700) / 40 = 3200 / 40 = 80. Column A = Column B = 80.
questions.trap: Students assume the weighted average will differ from the simple average even when group sizes are equal. Equal group sizes make weighted average identical to simple average.

questions.question: A solution is made by mixing 2 liters of a 30% acid solution with 3 liters of a 50% acid solution. What is the concentration of acid in the resulting mixture?
questions.explanation: Total acid: (2 × 0.30) + (3 × 0.50) = 0.60 + 1.50 = 2.10 liters. Total solution: 2 + 3 = 5 liters. Concentration = 2.10 / 5 = 0.42 = 42%.
questions.trap: Students average 30% and 50% to get 40%, ignoring the different volumes. The 3 liters of 50% solution outweighs the 2 liters of 30%, pulling the answer above 40%.

questions.question: A car travels 60 miles at 30 mph and then 60 miles at 60 mph. What is the car's average speed for the entire trip, in miles per hour?
questions.explanation: Average speed = Total distance / Total time. Time for first leg: 60/30 = 2 hours. Time for second leg: 60/60 = 1 hour. Total distance = 120 miles. Total time = 3 hours. Average speed = 120/3 = 40 mph.
questions.trap: Students compute (30 + 60)/2 = 45 mph using the simple average of the two speeds. For equal distances, the correct formula is the harmonic mean: 2 × 30 × 60 / (30 + 60) = 3600/90 = 40 mph.

questions.question: Group 1 has average value a and Group 2 has average value b, where a < b. Each group contains at least one member, and the two groups are combined into a single group. Which of the following must be true of the average of the combined group?
options: B. It is less than a
C. It is greater than b
D. It lies strictly between a and b
E. It is closer to a than to b
questions.explanation:
Write the combined mean as m = (n1 a + n2 b)/(n1 + n2), with n1 and n2 both at least 1.
Step 1 — lower bound. Every value in the sum is weighted against a and b, and since b > a, replacing b by a would lower the total. So m > a.
Step 2 — upper bound. By the same argument, replacing a by b would raise the total, so m < b.
Step 3 — therefore a < m < b, strictly, because both weights are strictly positive.
A is only true when n1 = n2. B and C are impossible by Steps 1 and 2. E is only true when Group 1 is the larger group, which is not stated.
Answer: D.
questions.trap: Choosing A, the plain average, which assumes equal group sizes. Choosing E is the other live error: the combined mean is closer to whichever group is BIGGER, and nothing here says Group 1 is bigger. Options B and C test the sanity check from the capsule: a weighted average can never escape the interval between the two group means.

questions.question:
Group X consists of 5 students with an average score of 60. Group Y consists of 15 students with an average score of 80.
Column A: The average score of all 20 students
Column B: 70
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — totals. Group X: 5 x 60 = 300. Group Y: 15 x 80 = 1200.
Step 2 — combined mean = (300 + 1200)/20 = 1500/20 = 75.
Step 3 — compare: 75 > 70, so Column A is greater.
Faster, no arithmetic: Group Y has three times as many students as Group X, so the combined mean must be pulled three quarters of the way from 60 to 80. That is well above the midpoint 70, which settles it immediately.
Answer: A.
questions.trap: Averaging 60 and 80 to get 70 and choosing C. The groups differ in size 5 to 15, so the midpoint is not the combined mean. Column B is exactly the number that error produces, which is why C is the tempting key.

questions.question: On a job site, 8 workers each earn $15 per hour and 2 workers each earn $25 per hour. What is the average hourly wage of the 10 workers?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — total wage bill per hour: (8 x 15) + (2 x 25) = 120 + 50 = 170.
Step 2 — divide by the number of workers: 170/10 = 17.
Check the pull direction: 8 of the 10 workers are on $15, so the mean must sit close to $15, only a fifth of the way up the $10 gap: 15 + (2/10)(10) = 17. Correct.
Answer: $17.
questions.trap: Choosing $20, the plain average of $15 and $25, which ignores that the $15 group is four times as large. Choice D, $23, is the same computation with the counts attached to the wrong wages (2 at $15 and 8 at $25). Choices A and E are the two wages themselves, picked by students who stop at 'most workers earn $15' or grab the larger rate.

questions.question: A student has grades of 85, 90, and 95 in three subjects. The weights of the subjects are 2, 3, and 5 respectively. What is the student's weighted average grade?
questions.trap: Students compute (85 + 90 + 95)/3 = 90, ignoring the weights. The subject with weight 5 (score 95) has the most influence, pulling the average above the simple mean of 90.

questions.question: A mixture contains 4 pounds of nuts costing $6 per pound and 6 pounds of nuts costing $9 per pound. What is the cost per pound of the mixture?
questions.explanation: Total cost: (4 × $6) + (6 × $9) = $24 + $54 = $78. Total weight: 4 + 6 = 10 pounds. Cost per pound = $78 / 10 = $7.80.
questions.trap: Students average $6 and $9 to get $7.50. But 6 pounds of the expensive nuts outweigh the 4 pounds of cheaper nuts, so the answer must exceed $7.50.

questions.question:
Alloy P is 20% gold. Alloy Q is 50% gold. Equal masses of P and Q are mixed together.

Column A: The percentage of gold in the mixture
Column B: 35%
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Since equal masses are mixed, the weighted average is the simple average: (20% + 50%) / 2 = 35%. Column A = 35% = Column B.
questions.trap: Students overcomplicate this by applying a weighted formula unnecessarily. When the two quantities (masses) being mixed are equal, the weighted average reduces to the simple average.

questions.question: In a school, 40% of the students are in Grade 9 and 60% are in Grade 10. The average GPA of Grade 9 students is 3.2, and the average GPA of Grade 10 students is 3.8. What is the overall average GPA of the school?
questions.explanation: Weighted average = (0.40 × 3.2) + (0.60 × 3.8) = 1.28 + 2.28 = 3.56. When weights are given as percentages (or fractions that sum to 1), we multiply each value by its weight fraction directly.
questions.trap: Students compute (3.2 + 3.8)/2 = 3.50, ignoring that Grade 10 has 60% of students vs Grade 9's 40%. The larger Grade 10 group pulls the average closer to 3.8.

questions.question: At a company, 25% of the employees work in the Delhi office and the remaining 75% work in the Mumbai office. In the Delhi office, 80% of the employees hold a graduate degree; in the Mumbai office, 40% do. What percent of all the company's employees hold a graduate degree? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
A percent is just an average of 1s and 0s, so the overall percent is the weighted average of the two office percents, weighted by head count.
Step 1 — set the total head count to 100 (legal, since only shares are given). Delhi has 25 employees, Mumbai has 75.
Step 2 — count graduates: Delhi 0.80 x 25 = 20; Mumbai 0.40 x 75 = 30.
Step 3 — overall: (20 + 30)/100 = 50/100 = 50%.
One line with fractional weights: 0.25 x 80 + 0.75 x 40 = 20 + 30 = 50.
Answer: 50.
questions.trap: Averaging 80 and 40 to get 60. Mumbai holds three quarters of the staff, so its 40% dominates and the answer must be much nearer 40 than 80. Answering 70 is the same slip with the weights swapped (0.75 x 80 + 0.25 x 40).

questions.question: An investor puts $2,000 in Fund A which returns 5% annually and $8,000 in Fund B which returns 10% annually. What is the weighted average annual return on the total investment?
questions.trap: Students average 5% and 10% to get 7.5%, ignoring the investment amounts. Fund B receives 80% of the total capital ($8,000 out of $10,000), making its return far more influential.

questions.question:
A class of 30 students took two tests. On Test 1, the average score was 70. On Test 2, the average score was 90. Test 1 is worth 60% of the grade and Test 2 is worth 40%.

Column A: The weighted average grade
Column B: 78
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Weighted average = (0.60 × 70) + (0.40 × 90) = 42 + 36 = 78. Column A = 78 = Column B.
questions.trap: Students compute (70 + 90)/2 = 80, or incorrectly multiply 0.60 × 90 + 0.40 × 70 = 54 + 28 = 82 (reversing the weights). Must match each weight to its corresponding test score.

questions.question: A car travels from City A to City B at 60 mph and returns at 40 mph. What is the average speed for the entire round trip?
questions.explanation: Let the one-way distance be d. Time going: d/60. Time returning: d/40. Total distance = 2d. Total time = d/60 + d/40 = 2d/120 + 3d/120 = 5d/120 = d/24. Average speed = 2d / (d/24) = 48 mph. Alternatively: harmonic mean = 2 × 60 × 40 / (60 + 40) = 4800/100 = 48 mph.
questions.trap: Students compute (60 + 40)/2 = 50 mph. For equal distances at different speeds, average speed is the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean. The car spends more time at 40 mph, dragging the average below 50.

questions.question: A weighted average of values V1 = 20 and V2 = 40 is computed using weights W1 and W2. Select all values that the weighted average CAN equal.
questions.explanation: The weighted average must lie between the smallest value (20) and largest value (40), inclusive. Any value in [20, 40] is achievable with some combination of non-negative weights. A=20 (all weight on V1, e.g., W1=1, W2=0), B=25 (W1=3, W2=1), C=30 (equal weights), D=35 (W1=1, W2=3), E=45 is outside the range [20,40] — impossible.
questions.trap: Students include E=45 thinking that large weights on V2=40 can exceed 40. The weighted average is bounded above by the maximum value (40) and bounded below by the minimum value (20).

questions.question: A cafe sells regular coffee at $3 per cup and premium coffee at $8 per cup, and sells nothing else. On Tuesday it sold 40 cups in total for $190. How many cups of premium coffee did it sell?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — let x be the number of premium cups, so 40 - x cups were regular.
3(40 - x) + 8x = 190
120 - 3x + 8x = 190
5x = 70, so x = 14.
Step 2 — check: 26 regular at $3 = $78, 14 premium at $8 = $112, and 78 + 112 = 190. Correct.
Alligation route: the average price was 190/40 = $4.75. Distance from $3 is 1.75; distance from $8 is 3.25. The counts are the INVERSE of these distances, so regular : premium = 3.25 : 1.75 = 13 : 7. Premium = (7/20) x 40 = 14.
Answer: 14.
questions.trap: Choice D, 26, is the number of REGULAR cups - it is what you get from the alligation ratio written the wrong way round (13 : 7 read as premium : regular), and also from solving for the wrong variable. Choice B, 20, comes from assuming the two counts must be equal because $4.75 lies between $3 and $8. Choice C, 24, is 190/8 rounded up, dividing the whole takings by the premium price; choice E, 38, is 190 divided by the $5 price gap.

questions.question: Three groups of students have average scores of 60, 75, and 90. The groups contain 5, 3, and 2 students respectively. What is the average score of all the students? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
The two-group formula extends to any number of groups: multiply each mean by its count, add, divide by the total count.
Step 1 — group totals: 5 x 60 = 300; 3 x 75 = 225; 2 x 90 = 180.
Step 2 — overall total: 300 + 225 + 180 = 705.
Step 3 — total students: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.
Step 4 — average: 705/10 = 70.5.
Check: the largest group sits at the lowest mean, so the answer must fall below the middle mean of 75. It does.
Answer: 70.5.
questions.trap: Averaging the three group means, (60 + 75 + 90)/3 = 75, which silently gives each group the same weight. Half the students are in the 60 group, so the true mean is dragged well below 75. Weighting by the group MEANS instead of the counts is the other version of the same error.

questions.question:
A mixture is made by combining Solution X (10% salt) and Solution Y (30% salt). The final mixture is 18% salt.

Column A: The ratio of Solution X to Solution Y in the mixture (by volume)
Column B: 2:3
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Let x = volume of X, y = volume of Y. Set up the weighted average equation: (10x + 30y)/(x+y) = 18. Multiply out: 10x + 30y = 18x + 18y → 12y = 8x → x/y = 12/8 = 3/2. So the ratio of X to Y is 3:2. Column A (ratio X:Y = 3:2 = 1.5) vs Column B (ratio 2:3 ≈ 0.667). Column A is greater. By alligation: distance from X (10%) to mean (18%) = 8; distance from Y (30%) to mean (18%) = 12. Ratio X:Y = 12:8 = 3:2, confirming X:Y = 3:2 > 2:3.
questions.trap: Students set up the alligation ratio in the wrong direction, computing X:Y = 8:12 = 2:3 (using the distances in the wrong order). The alligation rule is: ratio of quantity X to quantity Y equals the distance of Y's concentration from the mean to the distance of X's concentration from the mean.

questions.question: The average weight of 8 men is 72 kg and the average weight of 4 women is 60 kg. Four men and four women join the group. The average weight of the men in the enlarged group remains 72 kg and the average weight of the women remains 60 kg. What is the new overall average weight of all 20 people?
questions.explanation: New group: 12 men averaging 72 kg, 8 women averaging 60 kg. Total weight = (12 × 72) + (8 × 60) = 864 + 480 = 1344. Total people = 20. Overall average = 1344/20 = 67.2 kg. Closest answer is C = 67. Exactly: weighted average = (12/20)×72 + (8/20)×60 = 0.6×72 + 0.4×60 = 43.2 + 24 = 67.2.
questions.trap: Students compute the overall average as (72+60)/2 = 66 using equal weight for each group, ignoring the fact that there are now 12 men and only 8 women. The larger men's group pulls the average closer to 72.

questions.question: For real numbers a and b, define M = (3a + 5b)/8. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. If a < b, then M is closer to b than to a
B. If a is not equal to b, then M lies strictly between a and b
C. M > (a + b)/2 for all a and b
D. If a and b are each increased by 4, then M increases by 4
E. If a and b are each multiplied by 3, then M is multiplied by 3 and then increased by 8
questions.explanation:
M is a weighted average: the weights 3/8 and 5/8 are non-negative and sum to 1.
A - the distances are M - a = 5(b - a)/8 and b - M = 3(b - a)/8. When a < b both are positive and the second is smaller, so M is closer to b. TRUE.
B - both weights are strictly positive, so M is a strict convex combination of a and b and cannot reach either endpoint unless a = b. TRUE.
C - M - (a + b)/2 = (3a + 5b)/8 - (4a + 4b)/8 = (b - a)/8. This is positive only when b > a. Take a = 5, b = 1: M = (15 + 5)/8 = 2.5 while (a + b)/2 = 3, so M is smaller. FALSE.
D - adding 4 to both: (3(a + 4) + 5(b + 4))/8 = M + 32/8 = M + 4, because the weights sum to 1. TRUE.
E - multiplying both by 3: (3(3a) + 5(3b))/8 = 3M exactly. There is no extra 8. FALSE.
Answer: A, B, D.
questions.trap: C is the trap for anyone who reads 'the heavier weight sits on b' as 'M is always above the midpoint'. That holds only when b is the larger value; reverse the roles and M drops below the midpoint. E baits the student who has just used the shift rule in D and assumes scaling behaves the same way - a weighted average shifts by the shift but scales by the scale factor, with no additive leftover.

questions.question: A train travels the first 120 km at 60 km/h and the next 180 km at 90 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire journey in km/h?
questions.explanation: Time for first segment: 120/60 = 2 hours. Time for second segment: 180/90 = 2 hours. Total distance = 120 + 180 = 300 km. Total time = 2 + 2 = 4 hours. Average speed = 300/4 = 75 km/h. Note: since equal time is spent at each speed, the average speed equals the simple average: (60+90)/2 = 75.
questions.trap: Students apply the harmonic mean formula 2×60×90/(60+90) = 10800/150 = 72, which applies when EQUAL DISTANCES are covered. Here the distances are unequal (120 vs 180), so the basic formula Total distance/Total time must be used.

questions.question: A teacher weights homework at 20%, midterm at 30%, and final exam at 50%. A student scored 100 on homework, 70 on midterm, and 80 on the final. What is the student's weighted grade?
questions.trap: Students compute (100 + 70 + 80)/3 = 83.3 using a simple average. The weights (20%, 30%, 50%) must be applied to each component score.

questions.question:
A car drives from P to Q at a constant speed of v1 km/h and immediately returns from Q to P along the same road at a constant speed of v2 km/h. Both v1 and v2 are positive, and v1 is not equal to v2.
Column A: The car's average speed for the round trip
Column B: (v1 + v2)/2
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Average speed is never a weighted average of the speeds by DISTANCE - it is total distance over total time.
Step 1 — let the one-way distance be d. Total distance = 2d. Total time = d/v1 + d/v2.
Step 2 — average speed = 2d / (d/v1 + d/v2) = 2/(1/v1 + 1/v2) = 2 v1 v2/(v1 + v2), the harmonic mean.
Step 3 — compare with the arithmetic mean. (v1 + v2)/2 - 2 v1 v2/(v1 + v2) = ((v1 + v2)^2 - 4 v1 v2)/(2(v1 + v2)) = (v1 - v2)^2/(2(v1 + v2)).
Since v1 is not equal to v2, that numerator is strictly positive and the denominator is positive, so Column B is strictly greater.
Concrete check: v1 = 60, v2 = 40 gives average speed 2(60)(40)/100 = 48, while (60 + 40)/2 = 50.
Answer: B.
questions.trap: Choosing C, on the reasoning that half the trip is at each speed so the mean of the speeds must be the average speed. The two halves are equal in DISTANCE, not in TIME - the car spends longer on the slow leg, so the slow speed carries the heavier time weight and drags the true average below the midpoint. A weighted average of rates equals total-over-total only when the weights are the times, that is, the denominators of the rates.

questions.question: How many liters of a 60% salt solution must be added to 10 liters of a 30% salt solution to obtain a 40% salt solution?
questions.trap: Students use the alligation shortcut but mix up which distance corresponds to which solution. By alligation: distance of 60% solution from target 40% is |60-40|=20; distance of 30% solution from target 40% is |40-30|=10. Ratio = 10:20 = 1:2. So x liters of 60% : 10 liters of 30% = 1:2, giving x = 5.

questions.question: The average age of a group of 9 people is 30 years. One more person, aged 48, joins the group. What is the average age of the 10 people now? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
This is a weighted average of two groups whose sizes are 9 and 1.
Step 1 — convert the average to a total: 9 x 30 = 270.
Step 2 — add the newcomer: 270 + 48 = 318.
Step 3 — divide by the new count: 318/10 = 31.8.
Faster, using the excess: the newcomer is 48 - 30 = 18 years above the old mean, and that surplus is now spread over all 10 people, lifting the mean by 18/10 = 1.8. So 30 + 1.8 = 31.8.
Answer: 31.8.
questions.trap: Answering 39, the plain average of 30 and 48, which weights one newcomer as heavily as the nine people already there. The correct weights are 9 and 1, so the mean barely moves. The other slip is dividing the new total by 9 instead of 10.

questions.question: In a class containing at least one boy and at least one girl, the boys' average test score is 70 and the girls' average test score is 85. Which of the following could be the average score of the whole class? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
The class mean is a weighted average of 70 and 85 with strictly positive weights, so it must lie in the OPEN interval from 70 to 85.
A - 69 is below 70. No mixture of two groups can produce a mean below the smaller group mean. FALSE.
B - 72 is inside the interval; take many boys and few girls, for example 13 boys and 2 girls: (13 x 70 + 2 x 85)/15 = (910 + 170)/15 = 72. TRUE.
C - 77.5 is the midpoint, achieved with equal numbers of boys and girls. TRUE.
D - 84 is inside the interval; take 1 boy and 14 girls: (70 + 14 x 85)/15 = (70 + 1190)/15 = 84. TRUE.
E - 86 is above 85, impossible for the same reason as A. FALSE.
Answer: B, C, D.
questions.trap: Including A because 'a class that is nearly all boys could push the average below 70'. It cannot: adding girls at 85 can only pull the mean UP from 70, never past it. E is the mirror image of that error. Note also that the endpoints 70 and 85 themselves are unreachable, since the stem guarantees at least one student of each kind.

questions.question: In a school district, the boys' average math score is 72 and the girls' average math score is 78. The district's overall average math score is 76. What fraction of the students in the district are boys?
questions.explanation:
Method 1 — algebra. Let b be the fraction of students who are boys, so 1 - b are girls.
72b + 78(1 - b) = 76
72b + 78 - 78b = 76
-6b = -2, so b = 1/3.
Method 2 — alligation, and mind the direction. Distance from the boys' mean to the overall mean: 76 - 72 = 4. Distance from the overall mean to the girls' mean: 78 - 76 = 2. The group sizes are the INVERSE of these distances, so boys : girls = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2, and boys are 1/(1 + 2) = 1/3 of the district.
Check: (1/3)(72) + (2/3)(78) = 24 + 52 = 76. Correct.
Answer: 1/3.
questions.trap: Choice D, 2/3, is the alligation ratio written the right way round by luck and then inverted: 76 sits closer to 78, so the GIRLS must be the larger group and boys must be the smaller share. Always ask which mean the overall average is nearer, and give that group the bigger weight. Choice C assumes equal groups, which would give 75, not 76. Choices A and E come from measuring against the full spread 78 - 72 = 6 instead of the distance from each group's own mean, giving 2 : 6 and 6 : 2.

questions.question:
Solution A is 25% acid. Solution B is 75% acid. They are mixed to form Solution C, which is 50% acid.

Column A: Volume of Solution A used
Column B: Volume of Solution B used
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: By alligation: distance of A from target: |50-25| = 25. Distance of B from target: |75-50| = 25. Since both distances are equal, the volumes must be equal (ratio A:B = 25:25 = 1:1). Column A = Column B.
questions.trap: Students compute intuitively that since 50 is exactly between 25 and 75, the volumes are equal, but then second-guess themselves and choose D thinking there could be different amounts. The symmetry of the alligation gives a definitive 1:1 ratio.

questions.question: In a college, 30% of students are freshmen, 25% are sophomores, 25% are juniors, and 20% are seniors. Their average GPAs are 2.8, 3.0, 3.2, and 3.5 respectively. What is the overall average GPA of the college?
questions.trap: Students compute (2.8+3.0+3.2+3.5)/4 = 12.5/4 = 3.125, the simple average of the four GPAs. The unequal class sizes (30%, 25%, 25%, 20%) mean this is incorrect.

questions.question: A school has exactly three sections. Section A has 20 students with an average score of 68 and Section B has 30 students with an average score of 78. All 100 students in the school have an average score of 80. What is the average score of Section C?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — Section C's size. The school has 100 students and A and B account for 20 + 30 = 50, so Section C has 50 students.
Step 2 — the school total: 100 x 80 = 8000.
Step 3 — A and B totals: 20 x 68 = 1360 and 30 x 78 = 2340, so together 3700.
Step 4 — Section C's total: 8000 - 3700 = 4300, over 50 students, gives 4300/50 = 86.
Check: (1360 + 2340 + 50 x 86)/100 = (3700 + 4300)/100 = 80. Correct.
Shortcut: A and B together average 3700/50 = 74, and they are exactly half the school. Two equal halves average 80, so the other half must be 2(80) - 74 = 86.
Answer: 86.
questions.trap: Choice A, 74, is the combined average of Sections A and B - the right intermediate number reported as the final answer. Choice E, 94, comes from treating the three section means as equally weighted: (68 + 78 + x)/3 = 80 gives x = 94, which ignores that Section C is as big as A and B put together. Choice D, 92, is 80 + (80 - 68), adjusting for Section A's shortfall only.

questions.question:
Group A has an average score of 70 and Group B has an average score of 90. Group A has more members than Group B, and each group has at least one member.
Column A: The average score of Groups A and B combined
Column B: 80
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Let nA and nB be the two group sizes, with nA > nB > 0.
Step 1 — the combined mean is m = (70 nA + 90 nB)/(nA + nB). Rewrite it as m = 70 + 20 x nB/(nA + nB).
Step 2 — since nA > nB, the fraction nB/(nA + nB) is strictly less than 1/2.
Step 3 — therefore m < 70 + 20(1/2) = 80, no matter what the actual sizes are.
So Column B is greater. Two examples confirm it: nA = 3, nB = 1 gives (210 + 90)/4 = 75; nA = 100, nB = 99 gives (7000 + 8910)/199 = 79.95. Both below 80.
Answer: B.
questions.trap: Keying D because the individual group sizes are never given. They do not need to be: the single fact that Group A is the larger group fixes which side of the midpoint the combined mean falls on. The exact sizes are undetermined but the COMPARISON is determined, and that is all a QC asks. The opposite error is choosing C by averaging 70 and 90.

questions.question: Three sections P, Q and R contain students in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. Section P averaged 84 on a test and Section Q averaged 78. All the students in the three sections together averaged 77. What was Section R's average? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
Ratios can be used directly as weights, so let the sections have 3k, 4k and 5k students; the k will cancel.
Step 1 — total parts: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
Step 2 — write the weighted-average equation with R's mean as x:
(3 x 84 + 4 x 78 + 5x)/12 = 77
Step 3 — clear the denominator: 3(84) + 4(78) + 5x = 12(77).
252 + 312 + 5x = 924
564 + 5x = 924
5x = 360, so x = 72.
Check: (252 + 312 + 360)/12 = 924/12 = 77. Correct.
Answer: 72.
questions.trap: Solving (84 + 78 + x)/3 = 77 and answering 69, which weights the three sections equally even though R is the largest. The other slip is multiplying the overall mean by 3 instead of by 12: the right-hand side must be the mean times the TOTAL number of parts, not the number of groups.

questions.question: The average salary in Department A is $60,000 and the average salary in Department B is $90,000. When the two departments are combined, the average salary of all their employees is $72,000. If Department B has 12 employees, how many employees does Department A have?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — alligation, watching the direction. Distance from A's mean to the combined mean: 72 - 60 = 12. Distance from the combined mean to B's mean: 90 - 72 = 18.
Step 2 — the head counts are the INVERSE of these distances: nA : nB = 18 : 12 = 3 : 2.
Step 3 — with nB = 12, the ratio gives nA = 12 x (3/2) = 18.
Check algebraically: (18 x 60000 + 12 x 90000)/30 = (1,080,000 + 1,080,000)/30 = 2,160,000/30 = 72,000. Correct.
Sanity check on direction: $72,000 is nearer $60,000 than $90,000, so Department A must be the bigger department, and 18 > 12. Correct.
Answer: 18.
questions.trap: Choice A, 8, is the alligation ratio applied upside down (12 x 12/18), which would make the smaller department the one whose mean is closer to the combined mean - impossible. Choice B, 12, assumes equal departments, which would give an average of $75,000, not $72,000. Choice D, 30, is the combined head count rather than Department A's. Choice E, 36, reads the 3 : 2 ratio as 'A has three times as many as B'.

questions.question: A class of 24 students has a test average of 72. A second class, in which every student scored exactly 100 on the same test, is merged with the first. The second class contains at least one student, but its size is not given. Which of the following must be true of the merged class's average? Select all that apply.
options: C. If the second class also has 24 students, the merged average is 86
D. It is 86 regardless of the size of the second class
E. It is greater than 80 regardless of the size of the second class
questions.explanation:
The merged average is m = (24 x 72 + n x 100)/(24 + n) = (1728 + 100n)/(24 + n), where n is at least 1.
A - every added student scores 100, above 72, so the mean can only rise. Formally m - 72 = 28n/(24 + n) > 0. TRUE.
B - the 24 original students average below 100, so the merged mean is a weighted average of 72 and 100 with a positive weight on 72, hence strictly below 100. TRUE.
C - n = 24 makes the weights equal, so the mean is the midpoint: (1728 + 2400)/48 = 4128/48 = 86. TRUE.
D - 86 is the answer only for n = 24. For n = 1, m = 1828/25 = 73.12. FALSE.
E - take n = 4: m = (1728 + 400)/28 = 2128/28 = 76, which is below 80. FALSE.
Answer: A, B, C.
questions.trap: D is the headline error dressed up: averaging the two group means, 72 and 100, and calling the result the answer whatever the sizes are. E is the intuition that 'a batch of perfect scores must swing the mean a long way' - four perfect scores added to twenty-four students move the mean only from 72 to 76, because the weight on the new group is just 4/28.

questions.question: A student's grade point average is the sum of (grade x credit hours) over all courses, divided by the total credit hours. This term the student earned: Calculus, 3 credits, grade 3.0; Chemistry, 4 credits, grade 2.7; English, 3 credits, grade 3.5; History, 2 credits, grade 4.0. What is the student's grade point average, rounded to the nearest hundredth?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — quality points, course by course:
Calculus: 3 x 3.0 = 9.0
Chemistry: 4 x 2.7 = 10.8
English: 3 x 3.5 = 10.5
History: 2 x 4.0 = 8.0
Step 2 — total quality points: 9.0 + 10.8 + 10.5 + 8.0 = 38.3.
Step 3 — total credit hours: 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 12.
Step 4 — GPA = 38.3/12 = 3.1916..., which rounds to 3.19.
Sanity check: the heaviest course (4 credits) carries the LOWEST grade, so the GPA must fall below the plain average of the four grades, 3.30. It does.
Answer: 3.19.
questions.trap: Choice C, 3.30, is the plain average of the four grades, which gives the 2-credit History course the same say as the 4-credit Chemistry course. Choice D, 3.34, attaches the credit hours to the wrong courses (2, 3, 4, 3 read down the list). Choice E, 3.83, divides the 38.3 quality points by 10 instead of 12 - the weights must sum to the total credit hours. Choice A, 3.03, drops History from both the numerator and the denominator.

questions.question:
A store sold n items on Monday at an average price of $40 and m items on Tuesday at an average price of $60, where n and m are both positive. The average price of all the items sold over the two days was $52.
Column A: n
Column B: m
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — write the weighted-average equation and clear the denominator.
(40n + 60m)/(n + m) = 52
40n + 60m = 52n + 52m
8m = 12n
m = (3/2)n
Step 2 — since n > 0, m = 1.5n > n, so Column B is greater.
Alligation, with the direction checked explicitly: distance from Monday's $40 to the mean $52 is 12; distance from the mean to Tuesday's $60 is 8. The counts are the INVERSE of the distances, so n : m = 8 : 12 = 2 : 3, and m is the larger.
Sanity check: $52 lies nearer $60 than $40, so the $60 day must be the day with more items sold. Correct.
Answer: B.
questions.trap: Writing the alligation ratio as n : m = 12 : 8 and concluding n > m. The distances go with the OPPOSITE group: the 12 belongs to Monday's price but sizes the Tuesday count. The reliable check is the position of the mean - $52 sits closer to $60, so the $60 group is the heavier one. Keying D because neither n nor m is given individually is the other error; the ratio is fully determined even though the counts are not.

questions.question: The average score of 25 students on a test was 72. When the 5 lowest scores were excluded, the average of the remaining 20 students was 76. What was the average of the 5 excluded scores? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
The 25 students split into two groups of sizes 20 and 5, and their means combine to 72.
Step 1 — total for all 25: 25 x 72 = 1800.
Step 2 — total for the 20 who remain: 20 x 76 = 1520.
Step 3 — total for the 5 excluded: 1800 - 1520 = 280.
Step 4 — their average: 280/5 = 56.
Check by recombining: (20 x 76 + 5 x 56)/25 = (1520 + 280)/25 = 1800/25 = 72. Correct.
Faster, using the shift: removing the 5 lifted the mean of the remaining 20 by 4 points, a gain of 20 x 4 = 80 points, so the 5 removed scores were 80 points below where 5 average students would have been: 5 x 72 - 80 = 280, giving 56.
Answer: 56.
questions.trap: Answering 68, from 72 - 4, as though the excluded group sat 4 points below the mean because the remaining group sat 4 points above it. The 4-point lift was spread over 20 students but the shortfall is concentrated in only 5, so the excluded group is 4 x (20/5) = 16 points below 72, not 4. The other error is subtracting the averages directly, 76 - 72 = 4, and answering 4.

questions.question: On a certain airline, 80% of passengers travel in Economy and pay an average fare of $300; the other 20% travel in Business and pay an average fare of $1,200. The airline then raises every Economy fare by 10% and cuts every Business fare by 20%. The proportion of passengers in each class is unchanged. What is the new average fare per passenger?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — update each class's average fare separately.
Economy: 300 x 1.10 = $330.
Business: 1200 x 0.80 = $960.
Step 2 — re-weight by the (unchanged) passenger shares.
New average = 0.80 x 330 + 0.20 x 960 = 264 + 192 = $456.
Check: the old average was 0.80 x 300 + 0.20 x 1200 = 240 + 240 = $480, so the fare has fallen by $24, a 5% drop.
Why 5%: Economy and Business each supplied exactly half the old revenue ($240 of the $480), so the percent change in the average is the REVENUE-weighted average of the two percent changes: 0.5(+10%) + 0.5(-20%) = -5%, and 480 x 0.95 = $456. Percent changes must be weighted by revenue share, not by head count.
Answer: $456.
questions.trap: Choice D, $499, is the head-count-weighted version of that shortcut: 0.80(+10%) + 0.20(-20%) = +4%, and 480 x 1.04 = $499.20. It fails because the Business passengers, though only a fifth of the people, carry half the revenue. Choice A, $422, chains both multipliers onto the overall average (480 x 1.10 x 0.80). Choice E, $528, applies only the Economy rise. Choice C, $480, assumes the two changes cancel.

questions.question:
Team A has 12 players with an average age of 25 and Team B has 8 players with an average age of 30. Two players from Team A, both aged 28, transfer to Team B, and at the same time two players from Team B, both aged 27, transfer to Team A. No other players join or leave.
Column A: The average age of all 20 players on the two teams after the transfers
Column B: 27
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — the combined average before the transfers.
Team A total: 12 x 25 = 300. Team B total: 8 x 30 = 240.
Combined: (300 + 240)/20 = 540/20 = 27.
Step 2 — the insight. The transfers move players between the two teams but nobody enters or leaves the pool of 20. The sum of all 20 ages and the count 20 are both unchanged, so the overall average is still 27.
Step 3 — confirm by grinding it out anyway.
New Team A total: 300 - (28 + 28) + (27 + 27) = 300 - 56 + 54 = 298, over 12 players, average 24.83.
New Team B total: 240 - (27 + 27) + (28 + 28) = 240 - 54 + 56 = 242, over 8 players, average 30.25.
Combined: (298 + 242)/20 = 540/20 = 27. Correct.
Answer: C.
questions.trap: Computing the two new team averages (24.83 and 30.25), averaging them to get 27.54, and choosing A. That averages the averages of two unequal groups - 12 players against 8 - and the correct weighting brings it straight back to 27. Keying D because the individual ages are unknown is the other error: only the totals matter, and neither total changes.

questions.question: Group A has an average score of 62 and Group B has an average score of 74. Each group contains at least one member, and the average score of the two groups combined is exactly 70. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. Group B has more members than Group A
B. Group B has exactly twice as many members as Group A
C. Group A has more members than Group B
D. Group A has at least 4 members and Group B has at least 8 members
E. If Group A has 9 members, then the two groups together have 27 members
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — fix the ratio by alligation. Distance from A's mean to the combined mean: 70 - 62 = 8. Distance from the combined mean to B's mean: 74 - 70 = 4. The sizes are the INVERSE of the distances, so nA : nB = 4 : 8 = 1 : 2.
Confirm algebraically: 62 nA + 74 nB = 70(nA + nB) gives 4 nB = 8 nA, so nB = 2 nA.
A - nB = 2 nA and nA is at least 1, so nB > nA. TRUE.
B - nB = 2 nA exactly. TRUE.
C - contradicts A. FALSE.
D - the smallest case is nA = 1, nB = 2. Nothing forces 4 and 8. FALSE.
E - nA = 9 gives nB = 18, and 9 + 18 = 27. TRUE.
Answer: A, B, E.
questions.trap: C is the inverted alligation: 70 is closer to 74, so Group B is the LARGER group, not Group A. D reads the two alligation distances, 8 and 4, as if they were the actual group sizes; they are only a ratio, so any multiple of 1 : 2 works, including a single member in Group A.

questions.question: A factory makes only two kinds of bolt: standard bolts weighing 30 grams each and heavy-duty bolts weighing 60 grams each. Last week the average weight of all bolts produced was 45 grams. This week the factory produces twice as many heavy-duty bolts as it did last week while producing the same number of standard bolts as last week. What is the average weight of all the bolts produced this week?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — recover last week's production ratio from the average. Let s standard and h heavy-duty bolts.
(30s + 60h)/(s + h) = 45
30s + 60h = 45s + 45h
15h = 15s, so s = h.
(You can read this off without algebra: 45 is exactly midway between 30 and 60, and a weighted average sits at the midpoint only when the two weights are equal.)
Step 2 — this week the counts are s standard and 2h = 2s heavy-duty.
New average = (30s + 60 x 2s)/(s + 2s) = (30s + 120s)/(3s) = 150s/3s = 50 grams.
Check: heavy-duty bolts are now two thirds of output, so the mean should sit two thirds of the way from 30 to 60: 30 + (2/3)(30) = 50. Correct.
Answer: 50 g.
questions.trap: Choice A assumes doubling one group's output leaves the average alone - it cannot, because the heavier group's weight rises from 1/2 to 2/3. Choice C, 52.5, adds half the 30-gram gap to the old average of 45, as though 'twice as many' meant 'halfway further up'. Choice D, 54, comes from assuming heavy-duty bolts already outnumbered standard ones 2 to 1 last week and so run 4 to 1 this week. Choice E takes the new mean all the way to the heavy-duty weight, ignoring the standard bolts that are still being made.

questions.question: A firm has exactly two divisions. Division A has 300 employees: 40% are managers, who average $120,000, and the remaining 60% are staff, who average $70,000. Division B has 200 employees: 25% are managers, who average $130,000, and the remaining 75% are staff, who average $60,000. What is the average salary of all 500 employees of the firm?
questions.explanation:
This is a weighted average of weighted averages: collapse each division first, then combine the two divisions weighted by head count.
Step 1 — Division A's average.
0.40 x 120,000 + 0.60 x 70,000 = 48,000 + 42,000 = $90,000.
Step 2 — Division B's average.
0.25 x 130,000 + 0.75 x 60,000 = 32,500 + 45,000 = $77,500.
Step 3 — combine, weighting by 300 and 200.
(300 x 90,000 + 200 x 77,500)/500 = (27,000,000 + 15,500,000)/500 = 42,500,000/500 = $85,000.
Check by counting people instead. Managers: 120 in A plus 50 in B, total payroll 120(120,000) + 50(130,000) = 14,400,000 + 6,500,000 = 20,900,000. Staff: 180 in A plus 150 in B, total payroll 180(70,000) + 150(60,000) = 12,600,000 + 9,000,000 = 21,600,000. Firm payroll 42,500,000 over 500 people = $85,000. Correct.
Answer: $85,000.
questions.trap: Choice B, $83,750, averages the two division means, $90,000 and $77,500 - the headline error one level up, ignoring that Division A holds 300 of the 500 employees. Choice A, $82,500, is the same combination with the head counts swapped (200 on A, 300 on B). Choice D, $90,000, stops after Step 1 and reports Division A's average as the firm's. Choice E, $92,000, computes Division B's average as the plain average of $130,000 and $60,000, namely $95,000, and then combines correctly.

questions.question:
Every student at School X and at School Y takes the same annual exam. In 2019 the average score was 80 at School X and 84 at School Y. In 2020 the average score was 88 at School X and 92 at School Y. Each school had at least one student in each of the two years, but a school's enrollment in 2020 need not equal its enrollment in 2019.
Column A: The average score of all students at the two schools combined in 2020
Column B: 8 more than the average score of all students at the two schools combined in 2019
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation:
Let p be School X's share of the two schools' combined enrollment in 2019, and q be School X's share in 2020; both lie strictly between 0 and 1, and they need not be equal.
Step 1 — the 2019 combined average: 80p + 84(1 - p) = 84 - 4p.
Step 2 — the 2020 combined average: 88q + 92(1 - q) = 92 - 4q. That is Column A.
Step 3 — Column B = (84 - 4p) + 8 = 92 - 4p.
Step 4 — Column A minus Column B = (92 - 4q) - (92 - 4p) = 4(p - q), whose sign depends entirely on how the enrollment mix shifted.
Case 1: p = q = 0.5. Column A = 90, Column B = 82 + 8 = 90. Equal.
Case 2: p = 0.9, q = 0.1. Column A = 92 - 0.4 = 91.6; 2019 average = 84 - 3.6 = 80.4, so Column B = 88.4. Column A is greater.
Case 3: p = 0.1, q = 0.9. Column A = 92 - 3.6 = 88.4; 2019 average = 84 - 0.4 = 83.6, so Column B = 91.6. Column B is greater.
All three outcomes occur, so the relationship cannot be determined.
Answer: D.
questions.trap: Choosing C on the reasoning that both schools improved by exactly 8 points, so the combined average must also rise by exactly 8. That holds only if the enrollment MIX is unchanged, and the stem deliberately allows it to change. Shifting students toward the higher-scoring school between the two years adds an extra lift on top of the 8; shifting them the other way subtracts one. The weights, not just the group means, drive the combined mean.

questions.question: Three plants make identical widgets. Plant A produces 120 widgets per hour and runs for 5 hours; Plant B produces 200 widgets per hour and runs for 6 hours; Plant C produces 100 widgets per hour and runs for 2 hours. It costs $5 to make each widget at Plant A, $3 at Plant B, and $7 at Plant C. Taking all three plants together, what is the average cost per widget, in dollars? Enter your answer as a number.
questions.explanation:
The weights must be the number of WIDGETS, not the number of hours - the average is per widget, so widgets are what you are averaging over.
Step 1 — output of each plant: rate x hours.
Plant A: 120 x 5 = 600 widgets.
Plant B: 200 x 6 = 1200 widgets.
Plant C: 100 x 2 = 200 widgets.
Total output: 600 + 1200 + 200 = 2000 widgets.
Step 2 — total cost.
A: 600 x 5 = $3,000. B: 1200 x 3 = $3,600. C: 200 x 7 = $1,400.
Total: 3,000 + 3,600 + 1,400 = $8,000.
Step 3 — average cost per widget: 8,000/2,000 = $4.
Check the pull direction: Plant B makes 60% of all widgets at the cheapest rate, so the average must sit well below the middle cost of $5. It does.
Answer: 4.
questions.trap: Weighting by hours instead of output: (5 x 5 + 6 x 3 + 2 x 7)/13 = 57/13 = $4.38. That treats an hour at Plant C (100 widgets) as worth the same as an hour at Plant B (200 widgets). Averaging the three costs directly, (5 + 3 + 7)/3 = $5, is the plainer version of the same mistake. Whenever a rate is given per hour but the question asks per item, convert to item counts first.

questions.question: A portfolio is split among stocks, bonds and cash with weights wS, wB and wC, each strictly positive and summing to 1. Stocks return 12%, bonds return 6% and cash returns 2%, and the portfolio's overall return is exactly 7%. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
The portfolio return is a weighted average of the three asset returns, so there are two equations:
12 wS + 6 wB + 2 wC = 7 and wS + wB + wC = 1.
Step 1 — eliminate wC by substituting wC = 1 - wS - wB:
12 wS + 6 wB + 2(1 - wS - wB) = 7
10 wS + 4 wB = 5, so wB = (5 - 10 wS)/4.
Step 2 — back out wC: wC = 1 - wS - (5 - 10 wS)/4 = (6 wS - 1)/4.
Step 3 — positivity pins the range. wB > 0 forces wS < 1/2; wC > 0 forces wS > 1/6. So 1/6 < wS < 1/2, and every value in that range is achievable.
A - wS = 0.4 is allowed (then wB = 0.25, wC = 0.35, and 12(0.4) + 6(0.25) + 2(0.35) = 4.8 + 1.5 + 0.7 = 7). Since 0.4 > 1/3, this is not forced. FALSE.
B - at wS = 3/8 both wB and wC equal 5/16, so wB is not greater. FALSE.
C - wB + wC = 1 - wS, so the claim is wS < 1 - wS, that is wS < 1/2, which Step 3 guarantees. TRUE.
D - wS + wB = wS + (5 - 10 wS)/4 = (5 - 6 wS)/4, and this exceeds 1/2 exactly when wS < 1/2. TRUE.
E - wC = (6 wS - 1)/4 < 1/2 exactly when wS < 1/2. TRUE.
Answer: C, D, E.
questions.trap: A and B are picked on feel: 7% sits nearer the bond return than the stock return, so it 'looks like' stocks must be a small slice and bonds must beat cash. Neither is forced. The only hard constraint the two equations impose is 1/6 < wS < 1/2, and every option has to be tested against that whole interval, not against one comfortable example. Note that C, D and E are all the same statement wS < 1/2 in disguise.

questions.question: A train covers the first third of its route at a constant 20 km/h and the remaining two thirds of the route at a constant 60 km/h. What is the train's average speed for the whole route, in km/h?
questions.explanation:
Average speed is total distance over total time, never a distance-weighted average of the speeds.
Step 1 — let the route be 1 unit long, so the legs are 1/3 and 2/3.
Step 2 — times: (1/3)/20 = 1/60 hour and (2/3)/60 = 1/90 hour.
Step 3 — total time: 1/60 + 1/90 = 3/180 + 2/180 = 5/180 = 1/36 hour.
Step 4 — average speed = 1/(1/36) = 36 km/h.
Check with real numbers: a 180 km route means 60 km at 20 km/h (3 hours) and 120 km at 60 km/h (2 hours), so 180 km in 5 hours = 36 km/h. Correct.
Why it IS a weighted average, once the weights are right: the time shares are (1/60)/(1/36) = 3/5 and (1/90)/(1/36) = 2/5, and (3/5)(20) + (2/5)(60) = 12 + 24 = 36. A mean of rates equals total-over-total only when the weights are the denominators of those rates - here, the times.
Answer: 36.
questions.trap: Choice E, 46 2/3, is the headline error: weighting the speeds by DISTANCE, (1/3)(20) + (2/3)(60). The train spends most of its TIME on the slow third, so the slow speed must carry the heavier weight, not the lighter one. Choice A, 30, applies the equal-distance harmonic-mean shortcut 2(20)(60)/(20 + 60), which is only valid when the two legs are the same length. Choice C, 40, is the plain average of the two speeds. Choice D, 44, uses the correct time shares but attaches them to the wrong legs, (2/5)(20) + (3/5)(60).
